title: Researchers target prolactin receptors to treat lupus
content: Researchers at the University of California, Riverside, and City of Hope have discovered a new strategy for treating systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The approach focuses on correcting an imbalance in prolactin hormone receptors found on disease‑causing immune cells. By targeting these receptors, the team was able to lower inflammatory molecules and reduce harmful immune cells while leaving normal immune cells intact. This finding offers a potential therapeutic direction for managing lupus‑related kidney damage.
summary: Researchers at the University of California, Riverside, and City of Hope identified a new strategy for treating systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The strategy targets an imbalance in prolactin receptors in disease‑causing immune cells, reducing inflammatory molecules and harmful immune cells while preserving normal counterparts.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Hereditary lung and liver disease successfully treated for first time with gene correction
content: Alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATM) is a congenital metabolic disorder caused by a genetic defect that leads to the incorrect production of the protective protein alpha‑1 antitrypsin (AAT). The deficiency primarily damages the lungs and the liver, and can result in serious conditions such as pulmonary emphysema, liver fibrosis, or cirrhosis. In particularly severe cases, an organ transplant is the last resort. Currently, no curative treatment is available for this disorder.
summary: Alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATM) is a congenital metabolic disorder caused by a genetic defect that results in the protective protein alpha‑1 antitrypsin (AAT) being produced incorrectly. For the first time, the disease has been successfully treated using gene correction, offering a potential cure where previously only organ transplant was an option.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Medicare spending rises 5.9% per stay after private equity buys hospices
content:
The study found Medicare spending rose by 5.9% per hospice stay after private equity acquisition compared to similar for-profit hospices that were not acquired.

The increase was mainly due to longer stays; the average length of stay rose by 6.3 days.

The shift appears related to patients who use less daily care, with a significant rise in the share of patients with dementia and a larger share of patients discharged from hospice alive.
summary: Medicare spending rises 5.9% per stay after private equity buys hospices.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study Shows 9 of 10 Older Australians Applying for Aged Care Receive Welfare Payments
content: A new study by researchers at Flinders University and the South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute (SAHMRI) examined the financial circumstances, sources of income and homeownership of more than 920,000 older Australians who applied for aged care between 2010 and 2019. The average age of the cohort was 82. The analysis found that nine in ten older Australians applying for aged care receive social welfare payments. The research provides a large‑scale snapshot of the economic profile of the aging population seeking aged‑care services.
summary: Study Shows 9 of 10 Older Australians Applying for Aged Care Receive Welfare Payments.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Child dies of measles, New York's first measles death in 30 years
content: A child in rural northern New York died after contracting measles, the state’s first death from the disease in 30 years, state officials announced Monday.
summary: A child in rural northern New York died after contracting measles. State officials said it is the state's first measles death in 30 years.
author: Medical Xpress

title: WHO urged to review nitrate drinking water standards amid health risk concerns
content: Dozens of global health and environmental organizations urged the World Health Organization on Tuesday to revise its decades‑old standards for nitrate levels in drinking water. The groups argued that the current guidelines do not reflect recent scientific evidence about potential health risks.
summary: Dozens of global health and environmental organizations called on the World Health Organization to revise decades-old nitrate standards for drinking water. They argue the standards do not reflect recent scientific evidence about potential health risks.

content: Archaeologists have conducted toxicological examinations of mummified individuals sacrificed at mountain shrines throughout the Inca Empire. The analyses identified psychoactive substances that the victims ingested prior to their deaths, shedding light on the drugs used in the civilization’s principal sacrificial ritual.
summary: Archaeologists performed toxicological analysis on the mummified remains of people sacrificed at mountain shrines across the Inca Empire. The analysis revealed the psychoactive substances they consumed before their deaths.

content: An improved snow model now better captures winter thaws and runoff in the Northeast. Mountain snow there differs from the western United States because the region’s milder, more humid climate shapes winter conditions. Existing snow models often fail to reflect these distinct differences.
summary: The improved snow model more accurately captures winter thaws and runoff in the Northeast. It reflects the region's milder, more humid mountain climate that differs from the western United States.

content: A recent study indicates that a gas naturally produced by the human body could help treat skin and wound infections, potentially offering a new approach alongside conventional antibiotics.

title: Antarctica's Hidden Microbial Biodiversity Powers Its Ecosystems
content: Antarctica is often pictured as a land of penguins, seals, and whales. Yet most of its scientific marvels lie beneath the surface and can only be seen with a microscope. These unseen microbial communities form the foundation of Antarctic ecosystems, remaining largely invisible to most visitors.
summary: Many people imagine penguins, seals and whales when thinking of Antarctica. Most of Antarctica's scientific wonders are microbial communities that form the foundation of Antarctic ecosystems and remain largely invisible to visitors.

title: China Imports Millions of Donkey Hides from Africa Every Year, New Book Traces Drivers
content: A new book, China, Africa and the Market for Donkeys, by China‑Africa trade specialist Lauren Johnston, examines the surge in demand for donkey hides over the past 15 years—an increase the author says has been driven mainly by China. Johnston, who spent several years researching the trade, discusses her findings on the drivers and impact of the African‑to‑China hide market.
summary: Demand for donkey hides has grown exponentially over the past 15 years, mainly driven by China. Lauren Johnston, a specialist on China trade with Africa, spent several years researching the donkey trade and published the book "China, Africa and the Market for Donkeys."

title: Monarch butterflies get tiny trackers to help scientists follow their mysterious migration
content: Rebeca Quiñonez-Piñón and other scientists are attaching tiny tracking devices to hundreds of monarch butterflies to identify critical stopover locations. This effort aims to find these resting spots before they disappear, addressing the question Quiñonez-Piñón had as a child about where the insects stop for meals and rest during their North American migrations.
summary: As a child, Rebeca Quiñonez-Piñón wondered where monarch butterflies stop for a meal and a night's rest on their long migrations across North America. Now she and other scientists are attaching tiny tracking devices to hundreds of butterflies to find those critical stopover locations before they disappear.

title: Fire losses to U.S. buildings could nearly triple by 2060 without new protections
content:
New research from the University of Colorado Boulder's Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES) indicates that fire losses to U.S. buildings could nearly triple by 2060 without new protections. The study notes that fires in the U.S. are becoming faster, larger, and more dangerous, while people continue to develop and move into fire-prone regions.

According to the researchers, this increased risk to structures will occur if society does not act on climate change, manage vegetation, or transform how buildings are constructed and adapted to fire. The findings highlight the compounding nature of these factors as they approach midcentury.
summary: Fire losses to U.S. buildings could nearly triple by 2060 without new protections.
author: Phys.org

title: Crow experiments show vocal communication requires extra mental effort
content: Research indicates that for animals capable of vocalization, deciding to emit a sound involves multiple neural processes. These processes include controlling the timing of the sound, its loudness, and pitch, while also adaptively switching between vocalization and other behaviors in response to changing circumstances.
summary: Crow experiments suggest that switching to vocal communication requires extra mental effort. The experiments show that choosing to emit a sound involves controlling timing, loudness, pitch, and switching between vocalizations and other behaviors.

title: Columnist James Woodford Challenges Boiling Frog Myth with Backyard Evidence
content: Columnist James Woodford reports discovering evidence in his own backyard that challenges the scientific consensus that the "boiling frog" metaphor is a myth. The popular concept suggests frogs die from slow environmental warming because they fail to notice the change, a claim generally dismissed by science. Woodford’s personal observations, however, appear to support the validity of this long-debated analogy.
summary: The boiling frog metaphor claims frogs die when water heats slowly, but science calls it a myth. Columnist James Woodford says he has found evidence against the myth in his backyard.

title: Vibrating mattress and nitric oxide pills boost clearance of Alzheimer's protein
content: A study found that lying on a vibrating mattress for 40 minutes while taking two nitric‑oxide‑releasing pills increased the brain’s clearance of an Alzheimer’s‑related protein. The enhanced removal was observed through the brain’s waste‑disposal system.
summary: Participants lay on a vibrating mattress for 40 minutes while taking two nitric‑oxide‑releasing pills. The treatment increased clearance of an Alzheimer's‑related protein through the brain’s waste‑disposal system.
author: New Scientist

title: USC researchers reverse aging liver cells, cut Alzheimer’s protein in half
content:
USC researchers have discovered that rejuvenating liver cells may protect against Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease.  

In a study with rats, an experimental drug restored aged liver cells, halving the amount of an Alzheimer’s‑linked protein and lowering low‑density lipoprotein cholesterol to levels seen in younger animals. The treatment also reactivated a previously unknown communication system that enables liver cells to clear harmful substances from the bloodstream.
summary: USC researchers found that an experimental drug restored aging liver cells in rats, cutting levels of an Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half and bringing bad cholesterol down to youthful levels. The treatment also revived a previously unknown communication system that helps liver cells remove harmful substances from the bloodstream.
author: Science Daily

title: CERN's LHC Finds Big Bang Matter in Small Collisions
content:
Scientists at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider have reported new evidence that even relatively small atomic collisions can recreate the extraordinary state of matter that existed moments after the Big Bang. The findings suggest that these brief, high‑energy interactions produce quark‑gluon plasma, an exotic substance in which ordinary particles dissolve into their fundamental building blocks.

The quark‑gluon plasma forms at temperatures more than 100,000 times hotter than the center of the Sun, providing a unique laboratory for studying the early universe’s extreme conditions.
summary: Scientists at CERN's Large Hadron Collider have uncovered evidence that small atomic collisions can recreate quark‑gluon plasma, the state of matter that existed shortly after the Big Bang. The plasma reaches temperatures over 100,000 times hotter than the Sun's core, breaking ordinary particles into their fundamental components.

title: Scientists Discover Loophole That Could Allow Fast-Spinning Black Holes to Split
content: Scientists have discovered a possible loophole in the laws that normally prevent black holes from splitting apart, suggesting that extremely fast‑spinning black holes might divide into two. The finding raises the possibility of an entirely new black hole phenomenon that future telescopes could potentially detect.
summary: Scientists have discovered a possible loophole in the laws that normally prevent black holes from splitting apart. The finding suggests that extremely fast-spinning black holes might divide into two, a new phenomenon that future telescopes could detect.

title: Extra weight may be aging your brain faster than you think
content: A 24‑year study of more than 8,200 adults found that excess body weight may accelerate brain aging, leading to faster declines in memory, concentration, and decision‑making skills. The effect was strongest among people over 65, raising concerns about the long‑term effects of obesity on brain health.
summary: A major 24-year study involving more than 8,200 adults suggests that excess body weight may accelerate brain aging, leading to faster declines in memory, concentration, and decision-making skills. The connection was particularly strong among people over 65, raising concerns about the long-term effects of obesity on brain health.

title: Scientists find experimental drug for Alzheimer’s repairs DNA damage, cuts inflammation
content: Scientists discovered that a drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries can address key features of Alzheimer’s disease, including DNA damage and inflammation. The experimental treatment has already undergone initial safety testing in humans and may expedite therapies that target the disease’s root causes.
summary: Scientists discovered that a drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries can address several key features of Alzheimer’s disease, including DNA damage and inflammation. The experimental treatment has already undergone initial safety testing in humans, potentially allowing a faster route to disease‑targeting therapies.

title: Scientist Siddhartha Roy wins 2026 Maddox prize after Flint water controversy
content:
A new Guardian podcast features Dr Siddhartha Roy, who was a third‑year PhD student when Flint, Michigan’s water supply was found to contain dangerous levels of lead. Roy was part of a team of scientists that publicly disputed state and federal statements that the water was safe, and his role earned him local recognition as a hero.

The episode recounts how subsequent research questioned the earlier belief that Flint’s children had suffered permanent brain damage. Roy’s commitment to following the evidence, regardless of the reaction it provoked, was cited as the reason he received the 2026 Maddox prize, an award for individuals who defend science and evidence in the face of hostility. In the interview with Ian Sample, Roy reflects on his Flint experience and explains why his work led to the loss of personal friendships.

Listeners can also explore additional Guardian coverage of the Flint water crisis and support the outlet through the provided link.
summary: Scientist Siddhartha Roy wins 2026 Maddox prize after Flint water controversy.

title: 2026 Pacific Northwest sees heightened storm activity and rare annular typhoons
content:
The Pacific’s tropical cyclone activity has remained high since April 2026, when Sinlaku intensified to super typhoon strength and struck Micronesia, Guam, and the Northern Mariana Islands. By the end of October, the Northwest Pacific Basin still hosted active storms. On October 29, 2026, the EPIC camera aboard the DSCOVR satellite captured an image of Super Typhoon In‑fa near the Mariana Islands, while the remnants of Typhoon Champi moved toward Alaska amid a series of storms traversing the Bering Sea. In‑fa was the fifth typhoon to reach the Mariana Islands that year, and the MODIS instrument on NASA’s Terra satellite recorded the storm the following day, just west of the island chain.

In‑fa displayed characteristics of an annular tropical cyclone: a nearly circular shape, a large eye, and an absence of prominent outer rainbands. Annular storms are uncommon, representing only about 4 percent of tropical cyclones in the western North Pacific. Their eyes average roughly 45 kilometers in diameter, larger than the 25‑kilometer eyes typical of standard tropical cyclones, and they tend to maintain strength longer in unfavorable conditions. By the time EPIC captured In‑fa, the storm remained tropical, whereas Champi’s remnants had undergone extratropical transition and entered the Bering Sea’s storm track.

Extratropical cyclones differ from tropical cyclones by having cold cores and drawing energy from temperature contrasts between warm and cold air masses. They usually develop fronts and large comma‑shaped cloud bands. NASA meteorologist Gary Partyka noted that extratropical transitions often expand a storm’s wind field, covering a larger area even if wind speeds do not increase. In this case, Partyka suggested that Champi’s remnants likely intensified a midlatitude system over the Bering Sea, creating a large, comma‑shaped cloud pattern on October 30.

Champi’s transformation followed a destructive path across the West Pacific, where it reached maximum sustained winds of nearly 300 kilometers per hour, prompting some observers to label it one of the season’s strongest storms. The typhoon narrowly missed Taiwan and Guam but delivered damaging winds and heavy rains to those islands, as well as to parts of China and Japan. When its remnants reached Alaska, the state avoided catastrophic damage comparable to the October 2025 impact of ex‑typhoon Halong, though some areas experienced high winds, heavy rain, and snowfall. According to University of Alaska Fairbanks meteorologist Rick Thoman, Champi was the fourth ex‑typhoon to enter Alaskan waters in 2026, following Bang‑Lang, Dujuan, and Choi‑wan. Thoman noted that roughly 60 ex‑typhoons have impacted Alaska since 1970.

Partyka described 2026 as a “particularly active year” for Pacific tropical cyclones, increasing the likelihood that Alaska would be affected by storms that had transitioned extratropically. He cited the strong El Niño underway in the Pacific as a likely contributor to the heightened activity, noting that El Niño tends to steer storms northward toward Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Japan, and the Korean Peninsula. The Earth Observatory images used in this report were taken by Michala Garrison from DSCOVR EPIC and MODIS data via NASA EOSDIS LANCE and GIBS/Worldview.
summary: 2026 Pacific Northwest sees heightened storm activity and rare annular typhoons.
author: NASA News

title: APOD November 3 2026 Features Comet C/2025 R3 (PanSTARRS) and Rainbow Meteor
content:
The Astronomy Picture of the Day for November 3, 2026 showcases a photograph that juxtaposes comet C/2025 R3 (PanSTARRS) with a colorful meteor streak. The image was taken from Hautacam, France, in April and displays the comet’s ion tail in blue and a dust tail, while the meteor appears in the foreground with a rainbow‑like hue. The accompanying explanation notes that the meteor is not likely to have originated from the comet; the comet lies far behind the meteor’s path.

The text explains that meteors are typically sand‑sized rocky debris that burn up in Earth’s atmosphere, and the vivid coloration of the meteor may suggest a complex composition. It also highlights three meteor showers that are active this month. The Southern Taurids are reaching their peak over the next few days, followed by the Northern Taurids about a week later; both showers are linked to comet 2P/Encke. Additionally, the Leonids Meteor Shower, associated with comet 55P/Tempel‑Tuttle, is expected to peak in roughly two weeks.

The APOD entry credits the image to Eddy Metais and lists the site’s authors and editors as Robert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, and Keighley Rockcliffe. The service is described as a collaboration between the Astronomy Picture of the Day program, NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, NASA Science Activation, and Michigan Technological University.
summary: The Astronomy Picture of the Day for November 3, 2026 shows comet C/2025 R3 (PanSTARRS) captured from Hautacam, France, alongside a colorful meteor that likely did not originate from the comet. The article notes that the Southern Taurids, Northern Taurids and Leonids meteor showers will peak in the coming days and weeks.

title: Some agencies and tech CEOs begin using Trump’s “Super Intelligence” label
content:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order at the end of September that directs federal agencies to replace the term “artificial intelligence” with “Super Intelligence” (capitalized and abbreviated “SI”). The order’s rationale, as stated, is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that view.

Within a month, the new label has begun to appear on government solicitations, such as an Immigration and Customs Enforcement request for “SI‑powered” surveillance equipment for detention facilities. Several agency websites have silently swapped the terminology, and the National Institutes of Health now displays a banner warning visitors that both the old and new terms may be seen during the transition. However, the rollout has not been uniform: the Pentagon’s Project Meridian announcement used the former term, a Federal Trade Commission release employed “superintelligence” (lower‑case and uncapitalized), and recent Health and Human Services press releases show no sign of the change.

The rebranding effort is also extending beyond government. On October 27, President Trump criticized the Wall Street Journal for not using “Super Intelligence,” suggesting a future rule could ban “artificial intelligence” from government documents. Newsmax, despite describing itself as “supportive of the President and his policies,” likewise has not adopted the term.

Among technology leaders, the White House Accord on Super Intelligence was signed by six prominent executives: Sundar Pichai (Google), Dario Amodei (Anthropic), Mark Zuckerberg (Meta), Greg Brockman (OpenAI), Elon Musk (xAI), and Jensen Huang (Nvidia). CNBC’s analysis of third‑quarter earnings calls found that only Zuckerberg and Musk used “Super Intelligence” consistently; Zuckerberg’s company had already been using “superintelligence” since the prior year. Musk’s companies appear to use the term most frequently, and he pledged to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, though he still mixes “SI” and “AI” in his own posts. Executives from Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet continued to use “AI,” while Microsoft’s recent shareholder letter referenced the “Super Intelligence era.” Huang has referenced the term but also uses “AI.”

Federal agency heads are now required to draft a new legislative definition of “Super Intelligence” for presidential review by the end of the month, and government staff are spending time creating guides on how to navigate the rebrand. Critics note the potential cost in time and taxpayer dollars, while observers warn that making the terminology a loyalty test could polarize the emerging national conversation about AI, which many Americans consider a top election issue.
summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: Researchers propose reverse game theory to improve AI alignment incentives
content: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to create incentives for powerful AI models that make following the rules the most rational choice. As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all. Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution —a sort of moral code. The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions, and mislead their evaluators. Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage. An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay. In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood. A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms). Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically. The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer. A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?” Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says. During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right. There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers. Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s. Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he said. Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment. Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he says. “Are you aligned? I don’t know. Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.” One potential issue with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally. Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should. It’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable. AI models exhibit behaviors that seem more human than machine, and they can be swayed by subtle factors that are difficult to understand and explain. “Is it even reasonable to assume that they will respond to incentives?” asks Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing scientific discovery through computational methods, who has written about mechanism design and AI safety. “Obviously, AIs are not rational,” Morris says. “They’re just algorithms at work.” However, as economists have found with humans, treating them as if they’re rational could still be useful if it helps to predict and control their behavior. Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a “defense in depth” strategy for keeping AI models aligned—alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, not instead of them. But there are a lot of questions to be answered before the approach can be implemented in actual frontier models. It’s unclear, for instance, how these theories will apply to real models, or whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another in practice. Models could find loopholes that no one anticipated. (Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment on whether they are working on this.) Whatever these mechanisms look like, they will ultimately have to slot into the biggest mechanism of all: the free market. “We play by the rules of economics,” says Hazan. A more aligned model may be good for the world, but if it’s slower or more expensive than a less aligned one, does our current system of rules and regulations actually incentivize any of the frontier labs to release it? “It’s a mechanism that’s responsible for a lot of prosperity for humankind,” he says of the market, “but it could be ultimately responsible for something very terrible.” Perhaps the entities really in need of a better mechanism design are the labs themselves.
summary: A new approach called reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, seeks to design rules that make following human-aligned behavior the most rational choice for powerful AI models. Researchers including Stephen Morris and Elad Hazan propose mechanisms such as cross‑model prediction rewards, competitive pairings, and auditor‑solver dynamics to discourage sandbagging and encourage alignment.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: DEA classifies SR-17018, touted by opioid users for withdrawal relief, as heroin-like drug
content:
On Reddit and Discord, individuals who are addicted to opioids have reported that the compound SR‑17018 can alleviate withdrawal symptoms.  

The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration has classified SR‑17018 in the same schedule as heroin, despite the reported potential benefits.
summary: On Reddit and Discord, people addicted to opioids say SR-17018 can remove withdrawal symptoms. The DEA has placed SR-17018 in the same category as heroin.
author: Wired

title: NASA’s Swift Observatory set to reenter Earth’s atmosphere later this week
content: NASA’s Swift Observatory, a 3,200‑pound satellite, is slated to reenter Earth’s atmosphere later this week. The reentry zone is projected to be broad, encompassing portions of Africa, Australia, Southeast Asia and South America.
summary: NASA’s Swift Observatory, a 3,200‑pound satellite, is expected to reenter Earth’s atmosphere later this week. The reentry zone spans parts of Africa, Australia, Southeast Asia and South America.
author: Wired

title: Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar Says ICE Is Driving Historic Latino Voter Turnout
content: “I did a Latino community event [and said] we have to actually fucking vote to tell these motherfuckers to fuck off,” Nevada secretary of state Cisco Aguilar tells WIRED.
summary: ICE is reportedly motivating a historic increase in Latino voter participation. Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar said at a Latino community event that voters must turn out to push back against ICE, according to WIRED.
author: Wired

title: 42AI exits stealth with $62.5M funding and world model to predict human behavior
content: Here's a question straight out of sci-fi: What if AI could predict what you were going to do before you decided to, even in a completely new situation?
summary: 42AI has come out of stealth and announced a $62.5 million financing round. The company says its world model can predict human behavior.
author: TechCrunch

title: Apple warns of unprecedented memory chip price surge, says it will hit margins
content: Apple warned that memory‑chip prices are rising at an “unprecedented” pace, a development it said is forcing the company to compete with datacentres for supplies. The iPhone maker noted that a decision to raise its own product prices has mitigated part of the impact and that its revenues are stronger than expected. However, Apple told investors the higher chip costs will compress profit margins, and its shares fell in after‑hours trading following the announcement.
summary: Apple said memory chip prices are rising at an unprecedented level as it battles datacentres for supply. The company warned the higher costs will eat into profit margins and its shares fell in after‑hours trading.
author: Guardian Technology

title: CPS prosecutor cites fabricated case in high court, raising AI error concerns
content:
A senior Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) prosecutor, Ravinder Dhillon, cited an entirely made‑up legal precedent in a high‑court case. The case concerned whether a child should be prosecuted for raping his younger sister, and the court documents show Dhillon referenced a nonexistent precedent during the dispute.

The error has drawn fresh attention to the growing number of artificial‑intelligence‑related mistakes affecting court proceedings. It underscores concerns that AI hallucinations may be contaminating the justice system.
summary: Senior Crown prosecutor Ravinder Dhillon cited a non‑existent legal precedent in a high‑court dispute over prosecuting a child for raping his younger sister. The mistake, disclosed in court documents, has heightened concerns about AI‑generated hallucinations affecting the justice system.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Iran warns of new battlefield after US strike on Qeshm, raises defensive readiness
content: Parliament speaker Ghalibaf said “the ball is in America’s court to prevent war” as Iran reached its highest defensive readiness and Iranian outlets reported Tehran had updated its target bank to include US support bases in Europe under a “response without geographical limits”.
summary: Iran warns of new battlefield after US strike on Qeshm, raises defensive readiness.
author: Euronews

title: Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia shifted from Jan 2027 to late December due to security concerns
content: The Asian Football Confederation has moved the Asian Cup from January 2027 to late December, citing “exceptional circumstances” and travel disruptions. The decision follows Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia that forced the Dakar Rally and the WTA Finals to be cancelled or relocated.
summary: The Asian Football Confederation moved the Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia from January 2027 to late December. It cited “exceptional circumstances” and travel disruptions caused by Houthi attacks that forced the Dakar Rally and the WTA Finals to be cancelled or relocated.
author: Euronews

title: Could Texas turn blue? Democrat James Talarico takes on Republican establishment
content:
In Texas, a state traditionally dominated by Republicans, Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico is being positioned as a potential catalyst for a shift toward a blue electorate. Talarico, a former schoolteacher and Presbyterian seminarian, has entered the race with the hopes of achieving what many have regarded as unlikely.

Recent polling shows Talarico performing strongly against Republican Ken Paxton, the longtime state attorney general. Paxton’s campaign is reportedly affected by ongoing legal troubles that have cast a shadow over his candidacy.
summary: Could Texas turn blue? Democrat James Talarico takes on Republican establishment.
author: France 24

title: Cheese becomes France's most stolen food product amid organized crime
content: Cheese has been identified as France’s most stolen food product, a trend described as “cold, calculated crime.” The press review notes that the thefts are linked to organized criminal activity, indicating a rise in cheese‑related offenses among European gangsters. No additional details about the scale or specific incidents are provided beyond the characterization of the thefts as systematic and criminally motivated.
summary: Cheese is France's most stolen food product. The theft is described as cold, calculated crime.
author: France 24

title: Abdul El‑Sayed rallies Detroit voters ahead of crucial Michigan Senate race
content:
Abdul El‑Sayed, a doctor and former medical administrator, is campaigning for a U.S. Senate seat for the Democrats. He delivered a closing pitch to Michigan voters at the Majestic Theatre in Detroit, a venue located in one of America’s poorest communities.

El‑Sayed has attracted large crowds at rallies across Michigan, emphasizing his promise to make healthcare free for all Americans. The report was provided by FRANCE 24’s team in Michigan.
summary: Abdul El‑Sayed rallies Detroit voters ahead of crucial Michigan Senate race.
author: France 24

title: Republicans scramble as Democrats aim to control Congress in US midterms
content:
Republicans have launched a final push to avoid a predicted thumping in the U.S. midterm elections, while Democrats are seeking to win control of Congress.  

A Democratic‑controlled House would place the first real political constraints on President Donald Trump since his return to office in 2025, and polls show the Republican to be the most unpopular president in modern U.S. history. France 24 International Affairs Editor Kethevane Gorjestani reports from Washington, D.C.
summary: Republicans made a final push to avoid a predicted thumping in the US midterm elections, as Democrats seek to win control of Congress. A Democratic-controlled House would impose the first real political constraints on President Donald Trump since he returned to office in 2025.
author: France 24

title: Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site kills 29, leaves 48 missing
content:
The death toll from a Russian attack on a humanitarian‑aid site in southern Ukraine rose to 29 on Tuesday, with 48 people still missing, officials said. The strike hit a location where civilians had gathered for assistance and was part of a broader wave of overnight attacks that hit power plants, damaged hospitals and wounded scores of people across the country.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that Russia launched 289 attack drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles in nine regions, causing emergency power cuts. The incident was covered by France 24’s Emmanuelle Chaze from Kyiv.
summary: Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site kills 29, leaves 48 missing.
author: France 24

title: Farmers near Biltine in Wadi Fira assess losses as drought intensifies
content: In Chad, the Wadi Fira region—one of the two hardest‑hit by the current drought—is seeing farmers just outside the regional capital Biltine assess the damage to their crops. FRANCE 24’s Harold Girard reports that the losses are described as devastating.
summary: Wadi Fira is one of the two regions hardest hit by the drought in Chad. Farmers a few kilometres outside the regional capital Biltine are taking stock of their devastating losses, FRANCE 24's Harold Girard reports.
author: France 24

title: DR Congo opposition leader Prince Epenge arrested on fake news charges
content: DR Congo senior opposition leader Prince Epenge has been arrested, transferred to prison and is being held on charges of spreading fake news, according to France 24’s Kinshasa correspondent Emmet Livingstone.
summary: Prince Epenge, a senior opposition leader in DR Congo, was arrested and transferred to prison. He is being held on charges of spreading fake news.
author: France 24

title: Arizona food stamp cuts become key issue in US midterm elections
content:
Arizona, a key battleground state in the US midterm elections, is experiencing significant disruption to its social safety net following the passage of President Donald Trump’s tax and spending law last year. Approximately half of the state’s food stamp recipients have lost their benefits, representing the steepest decline in the nation. State officials acknowledge that some of these individuals likely remain eligible, and the resulting errors have led to a sharp increase in food insecurity.

The consequences of these benefit cuts have emerged as a major issue on the campaign trail. As the state grapples with the fallout from the federal overhaul, the crisis in food assistance is now a central topic for candidates competing in the upcoming elections.
summary: Arizona, a battleground state in the US midterm elections, is at the centre of a sweeping overhaul of America's social safety net. Since US President Donald Trump's tax and spending law passed last year, about half of the state's food stamp recipients have lost their benefits – the steepest drop in the country.
author: France 24

title: US voters elect new Congress in midterm election, seen as judgment on Trump
content: US voters are casting ballots to elect a new Congress. According to the source, the outcome will be decisive for the United States’ future and will serve as a judgment on Donald Trump’s second term as president.
summary: US voters are electing a new Congress. The results are expected to be decisive for the United States and a judgment on Donald Trump's second term as president.
author: DW World

title: US tech giants' AI bond issuances pressure European governments' borrowing costs
content: France, Germany and Italy are confronting a volatile bond market as war‑related inflation pressures persist. At the same time, U.S. technology companies have begun issuing billions of dollars in AI‑linked bonds, positioning themselves as competitors for financing against cash‑strapped European governments, a dynamic that could increase the cost of borrowing in Europe.
summary: France, Germany and Italy face a volatile bond market as war inflation bites. US tech giants are issuing billions in AI bonds, competing with cash‑strapped European governments.
author: DW World

title: UK ministers told not to engage with Indian mega‑zoo Vantara ahead of CITES meeting
content:
Guardian and Mongabay reports that British government ministers were advised not to engage formally with Vantara, a controversial mega‑zoo operated by Indian billionaire Anant Ambani. The directive followed lobbying efforts by the private animal sanctuary in the lead‑up to a UK‑chaired meeting on the trade in endangered species. Documents show the lobbying was aimed at influencing the upcoming CITES committee session.

This week the United Kingdom is chairing a 32‑country CITES meeting in Geneva. The meeting will examine how India has responded to compliance concerns regarding imports of endangered animals.
summary: British government ministers were told not to engage formally with Vantara, the controversial mega‑zoo run by Indian billionaire Anant Ambani, after lobbying by the private animal sanctuary. The warning came ahead of a UK‑chaired CITES meeting in Geneva that will examine India’s response to compliance concerns about endangered‑animal imports.
author: Guardian World

title: Denmark seeks EU ban on ‘turbo chickens’ after secret footage sparks outrage
content: Denmark’s government is seeking a national ban on “turbo chickens” and is urging an EU‑wide prohibition of the fast‑growing breed. A minister said the administration will work toward banning the chickens across the country and Europe after secret footage sparked widespread outrage over alleged law‑breaking by a major Danish chicken producer.
summary: A Danish minister said the government will work towards banning the fast‑growing “turbo chickens” breed nationally and throughout the EU. The move follows widespread outrage over allegations of lawbreaking by one of Denmark’s big chicken producers.
author: Guardian World

title: UK and EU finalize deal to end Brexit checks on food and animal products
content:
The UK and EU have agreed to a deal removing Brexit checks on food and animal product imports and exports, including items such as sausages, cheese, leather goods, and flowers. The agreement is expected to come into force in the first quarter of 2028. This move aims to ease trade rules that were introduced in 2022.

The deal is anticipated to benefit British food exporters, whose trade with Europe has declined by a third since 2019. Additionally, it will allow smaller UK retailers, such as delicatessens, to resume purchasing smaller batches of cheese and wines, a practice that had become unfeasible due to the costs associated with the previous checks.
summary: UK and EU finalize deal to end Brexit checks on food and animal products.
author: Guardian World

title: Warsaw Modlin Airport Resumes Operations After Bomb Threat, Section Remains Closed
content:
Warsaw Modlin airport announced that it has resumed operations after an earlier bomb threat linked to a flight from London. Security forces continue to inspect the area of the terminal where the aircraft was parked, and that portion of the airport remains closed.

In a separate development, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his discussions with German Economy Minister Robert Merkel and President Frank Steinmeier will concentrate on diplomatic coordination of air‑defence and energy matters, emphasizing security, stability and the rules‑based international order.
summary: Warsaw Modlin airport said it has resumed operations after an earlier bomb threat. A part of the airport where the London flight was parked remains closed while security forces check it.
author: Guardian World

title: Reddit sues over Australia’s under‑16 social media ban, says it curtails political speech
content:
Reddit has taken the Australian government to the High Court, arguing that the 2024 legislation banning social‑media access for users under 16 infringes the implied freedom of political communication for teenagers. Lawyers for the platform told the court on Tuesday that the law was “ill‑thought‑out, over‑broad” and that it has been narrowed only after Reddit’s legal challenge.

The company, which ranks among the world’s ten most‑visited websites, maintains that the ban restricts political discourse among under‑16s and is therefore unconstitutional.
summary: Reddit has challenged the Australian government’s under‑16 social media ban in the High Court, arguing it impinges the implied freedom of political communication for teens. Lawyers described the legislation as ill‑thought‑out and over‑broad and noted it has been narrowed after Reddit sued.
author: Guardian World

title: Mater hospitals in Queensland close pathology labs amid formaldehyde probe
content:
In Queensland, a major hospital’s in‑house pathology services are shutting down permanently. The decision comes amid an investigation into possible formaldehyde exposure and ongoing financial pressure on the pathology business.

The closure will affect about 400 staff at both Mater’s Brisbane and Springfield hospitals. It also involves the laboratory that processes foetus and newborn tissue and cell tests for unexpected deaths.
summary: In-house pathology services at Mater’s Brisbane and Springfield hospitals in Queensland will permanently close. The shutdown, affecting about 400 staff and the lab that tests foetal and newborn tissue for unexpected deaths, comes amid a potential formaldehyde exposure investigation and continual financial strain.
author: Guardian World

title: Australia to review UK backpacker visa agreement after surge in British visitors
content:
Australia says that recent easing of visa rules has sparked a surge in British visitors, creating pressure on the local workforce. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told UK Labour leader Andy Burnham that the government is reviewing the arrangements for British backpackers after a rise in travellers to destinations such as Sydney.

Albanese made the comments following a meeting with Burnham on Monday evening at the Commonwealth heads‑of‑government meeting in the Caribbean. He said he will seek to discuss amending the UK‑Australia agreement that currently removes a regional work‑requirement for British travellers.
summary: Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he is looking to change visa rules for British backpackers following an increase in UK visitor numbers. He discussed amending the agreement that removes a regional work requirement with UK minister Andy Burnham at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in the Caribbean.
author: Guardian World

title: ‘I am deeply sorry’: Craig Silvey pens 9,000-word apology for child exploitation material offences
content:
Craig Silvey, the best‑selling author of young adult novels, was sentenced on Monday to seven months’ imprisonment for child exploitation offences. He had been charged in January and pleaded guilty to distributing and possessing depraved child‑exploitation material.

Following his sentencing, Silvey released a 9,000‑word apology in which he claimed he had experienced trauma as a child. The apology was published after he was jailed, and the article includes a warning about graphic content.
summary: ‘I am deeply sorry’: Craig Silvey pens 9,000-word apology for child exploitation material offences.
author: Guardian World

title: Laura Pannack wins inaugural Tom Stoddart award for South African youth project
content:
British visual artist and photographer Laura Pannack has been named the winner of the inaugural Tom Stoddart award for excellence 2025. The award, a collaboration between Gost Books and the Ian Parry photojournalism grant, supports photographers engaged in long-form documentary work.

Pannack’s project, Crossings, examines the journey to and from school and its physical and psychological challenges for young people in South Africa, a country noted for high social inequality and a rapidly growing youth population. The work is available now.
summary: British photographer Laura Pannack won the 2025 Tom Stoddart award for excellence for her documentary project Crossings. The project examines the physical and psychological challenges of the journey to and from school for young people in South Africa.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Yaga review: Hudson Williams stars in erotic witchy thriller as two characters
content: The Heated Rivalry actor plays two people in this genre-bending mystery. And Carrie-Anne Moss is fantastic as a horny author – who might have supernatural powers Well, here’s an unexpected answer to the question of what Hudson Williams did next: the overnight megastar created by the smash-hit success of Heated Rivalry (hot young men bang each other for seven episodes, emotional connection also glossed, intermittent hockey scenes) appears as two characters in the spooky thriller Yaga. Williams plays Henry Park, the missing scion of a powerfully rich family in the spooky Canadian coastal town of Whittock, and Henry’s spookily looky-likey roommate Logan, who lives in the Parks’ staffed mansion rent-free in return for helping Henry with his podcasts, parties and possible bisexuality. There is a lot of all three about these days among the young, I’m told. Usually by their podcasts.
summary: The film Yaga is an erotic witchy thriller in which Hudson Williams plays both Henry Park, a missing scion of a rich family, and his roommate Logan in a spooky Canadian coastal town. Carrie‑Anne Moss also appears as a horny author who might have supernatural powers.
author: Guardian Culture

title: De La Soul’s Pos reveals his off‑beat music favorites, from Barry White to Al Green
content: Rapper Pos of the hip hop greats favours Barry White for the bedroom and sobs to Stevie Wonder, but which cheese-rock hit does he love on the sly? The first song I fell in love with My father could sing really well – he was in a choir and had this coolness. He would walk around singing Love and Happiness by Al Green and, because he looked so much like him on the cover, I actually thought he was Al Green. The first single I bought Underlove by Melba Moore from Abraham & Straus, this department store in Long Island that had a mini record store inside. I later realised it was produced by Kashif, and I would fall in love with everything he produced.
summary: De La Soul’s Pos reveals his off‑beat music favorites, from Barry White to Al Green.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Nuno Espírito Santo under threat at West Ham after dropping to eighth in Championship
content:
West Ham manager Nuno Espírito Santo’s future at the club is under threat following a disappointing start to the Championship season. The team, which entered the campaign as promotion favourites, dropped to eighth place after suffering a 3-1 defeat to West Bromwich Albion on Saturday. This result marked the club’s second consecutive home loss, leaving them in the final playoff position and four points behind second-placed Swansea.

Despite the setback, West Ham remains intent on an immediate return to the Premier League after Nuno failed to prevent relegation in the previous season. While the manager is expected to be given time to improve the team’s performance, key figures within the club have reportedly grown increasingly impatient with the current results. The pressure on Espírito Santo was further highlighted by unrest from supporters during the match against West Brom.
summary: West Ham manager Nuno Espírito Santo's future is under threat after the team dropped to eighth in the Championship following a 3-1 loss to West Bromwich Albion. Key figures at the club are losing patience with the manager as the team trails second-placed Swansea by four points.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Led by Liam Rosenior and backed by billionaires, Paris FC are now a force in Ligue 1 | Luke Entwistle
content:
Pierre Ferracci, who has led Paris FC since 2012 after joining the club in 2006, recently presided over the final game of his tenure. During this match against Monaco, Ferracci stood among bare-chested Paris FC ultras who were singing his name. He admitted to missing the first 15 minutes of the game while interacting with the supporters. The scene highlighted the significant progress the club has made since Ferracci’s arrival, when the team was competing in the amateur third tier of French football. Ferracci initially took on an administrative role before assuming the positions of owner and president in 2012, with the club not reaching Ligue 2 until 2016.

The article notes that Paris FC is now considered a force in Ligue 1, a status bolstered by a significant summer period and the decline of other rivals to Paris Saint-Germain. Backed by billionaires and led by Liam Rosenior, the club is aiming to become one of the biggest in Europe.
summary: Led by Liam Rosenior and backed by billionaires, Paris FC are now a force in Ligue 1 | Luke Entwistle.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Arsenal have everything they need to repeat as Premier League champions | Jonathan Wilson
content:
Jonathan Wilson argues that Arsenal possess the necessary depth and experience to repeat as Premier League champions, a view supported by their recent victory at Liverpool. The Gunners currently lead the table by three points, though Wilson notes that their five-point gap over Brighton in third is more significant, as second-placed Manchester City face a likely major points deduction.

During Sunday’s match, Liverpool dominated for a 20-minute spell before half-time, creating an atmosphere reminiscent of Jürgen Klopp’s era at Anfield. However, Arsenal reset at the break and controlled the second half with relative ease. This performance marked the second consecutive league game in which they denied Liverpool a shot on target, reinforcing Wilson’s assessment that the team is navigating a weaker class of contenders than last season.
summary: Arsenal have everything they need to repeat as Premier League champions | Jonathan Wilson.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Andy Madley and VAR praised for correct Anfield penalty decisions
content: Timber’s shirt pull on Isak was not a penalty on review, and Madueke’s clash with Mac Allister was clearly not violent conduct There was one incident that got everyone talking at the weekend, and that was the decision not to award Liverpool a penalty in their match against Arsenal after Alexander Isak had his shirt pulled by Jurriën Timber as he tried to get his head to a Bradley Barcola cross. The on-field decision from the referee, Andy Madley, was no penalty and it was a call backed by the video assistant referee, Stuart Attwell. After the match the Liverpool head coach, Andoni Iraola, said there had been a “clear, clear pull” and when the footage is slowed down or freeze‑framed, that looks to be true. But at full speed, the contact appears minimal and not sustained: Timber is using one hand and tugs briefly on the shirt, and the impact on Isak’s movement is arguable.
summary: Referee Andy Madley and VAR Stuart Attwell correctly ruled that Jurriën Timber's shirt pull on Alexander Isak was not a penalty. The officials also accurately determined that Madueke's clash with Mac Allister did not constitute violent conduct.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Liverpool fail to register shot on target in 1-0 loss to Arsenal at Anfield
content:
Liverpool recorded their first Premier League match at Anfield without a shot on target since records began in 2003-04, following a 1-0 defeat to Arsenal on Sunday. According to Opta data, the team also failed to find the target in a previous goalless draw at the Emirates Stadium, though they struck the woodwork in both encounters.

The article highlights a significant efficiency issue for Andoni Iraola’s side, noting that the team made 52 touches within the Arsenal penalty area but generated only one Opta-defined big chance. This performance contrasts sharply with the Premier League average, which stands at 10.3 box touches per big chance. The piece suggests that while Arsenal restricted opportunities, Liverpool must learn to break down low defensive lines to improve their attacking output.
summary: Liverpool recorded zero shots on target in their 1-0 defeat by Arsenal, a statistical first for the club at Anfield since records began in 2003-04. Despite 52 touches in the penalty area, the team created only one big chance, a level of efficiency far below the Premier League average.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Wolff praises F1 champion Antonelli as role model
content: Mercedes team principal hits out at ‘selfish’ drivers Antonelli says he will keep No 12 on his car next season The Mercedes team principal, Toto Wolff, has described his Formula One world champion Kimi Antonelli as a new kind of racing driver who represents the future of the sport, com­paring him scathingly to what he called some of the entitled ­moaners on the grid and declaring “selfless, ruthless” drivers now dead to F1. Antonelli secured his first world title in Mexico City on Sunday, at 20 years old becoming the ­youngest F1 champion in only his second season in the sport. The ­Italian’s attitude, enthusiasm and sense of fair play have been notable in a revelatory season for a driver so young and Wolff believes he has proved to be a gamechanger in more ways than one.
summary: Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff described Formula One world champion Kimi Antonelli as a new kind of driver and role model. Wolff contrasted Antonelli's attitude with what he called entitled moaners on the grid.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Jaissle criticizes referee over 'clear foul' before Barry goal
content: Newcastle United head coach Matthias Jaissle criticized referee John Brooks for failing to award a "clear foul" on Fabian Schar during the build-up to Thierno Barry's goal. The incident occurred in the Premier League match where Newcastle lost to Everton.
summary: Newcastle United head coach Matthias Jaissle is unhappy with referee John Brooks' decision not to call a "clear foul" on Fabian Schar. The incident occurred in the build-up to Thierno Barry's goal in their Premier League loss to Everton.
author: BBC Sport

title: Moyes tight-lipped on Grealish availability after Everton win
content: Everton manager David Moyes provided a post-match reaction to his team’s one-goal victory over Newcastle United. He remained tight-lipped regarding the availability of Jack Grealish, who is facing disciplinary action.
summary: Everton manager David Moyes was tight-lipped regarding Jack Grealish's availability following disciplinary action. This occurred after his team secured a one-goal win against Newcastle United.
author: BBC Sport

title: Moyes confirms Grealish can still have Everton future
content: Everton manager David Moyes stated that Jack Grealish still has a future with the club. However, Moyes indicated that he is uncertain about when the player might return to the team.
summary: Everton manager David Moyes stated that there is a path for Jack Grealish to return to the team. He noted that he does not know when Grealish might return to the squad.
author: BBC Sport

title: Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle booed by fans after defeat
content: Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle faces growing criticism three months into his four-year contract, as his team was booed off the pitch by supporters following another defeat.
summary: Matthias Jaissle is facing growing problems at Newcastle after three months into his four-year contract. His team was booed off the pitch by their own supporters following another defeat.
author: BBC Sport

title: Duckworth condemns Trump’s low Halloween flyover, demands answers
content: Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) condemned President Trump’s recent low flyover in a letter sent on Monday to FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, OMB Director Russell Vought, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The incident took place Thursday during the White House’s Halloween party.
summary: Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) on Monday condemned President Trump’s recent low flyover in a letter addressed to Bryan Bedford, the administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA); Russell Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget; and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
author: The Hill

title: Cook Political Report Rates Michigan Senate Race as Lean Democrat in 2026 Midterm
content: The nonpartisan political handicapper Cook Political Report has shifted its rating of the 2026 Michigan Senate race to lean Democratic. In a post Monday on the social platform X, the Cook Political Report said it was “issuing its final Senate ratings of the 2026 midterm cycle” and that “the Michigan Senate race moves from Toss…
summary: The Cook Political Report has moved the 2026 Michigan Senate race from Toss to lean Democratic in its final midterm ratings. The change was announced in a Monday post on the social platform X.
author: The Hill

title: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed proposes S--- Lettuce Elimination Act
content: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) told reporters that if he was elected to the upper chamber, he wanted to pass an act related to 2026’s cyclospora outbreak: The S‑‑‑ Lettuce Elimination Act. “For a long time here in Michigan, right, over the summer, there were a lot of people who ate lettuce and then…
summary: Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic candidate for the Michigan Senate, said he would introduce the S--- Lettuce Elimination Act if elected. He linked the proposal to the 2026 cyclospora outbreak involving lettuce consumption.
author: The Hill

title: Senate Democrats accuse X of favoring Polymarket
content: Senate Democrats accused Elon Musk’s X of providing “preferential treatment” to the prediction market Polymarket on its timeline. In a letter sent Friday to X leadership, Democratic Senators Catherine Cortez Masto, Jacky Rosen, Adam Schiff, and Richard Blumenthal included screenshots alleging that the platform does not treat Polymarket equally.
summary: A group of Senate Democrats accused Elon Musk's X of giving the prediction market Polymarket preferential treatment on its timeline. The senators sent a letter to X leadership including screenshots that appear to show this bias.
author: The Hill

title: Talarico says he wants to work with Trump on bipartisan MAGA agenda
content: Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico stated his intention to collaborate with President Donald Trump on a bipartisan “Make America Great Again” agenda. During an interview, Talarico expressed his desire, as the next U.S. Senator from Texas, to work with Trump to fulfill promises associated with his political project.
summary: Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico stated he would want to work with President Trump on a bipartisan “Make America Great Again” agenda. He expressed his desire to fulfill some of the promises of Trump's political project during an interview.
author: The Hill

title: US to mediate Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi next week, Witkoff says
content: Special Envoy Steve Witkoff announced that the United States will mediate working-level negotiations between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi on November 10–11. Witkoff stated on the social platform X that these talks aim to advance President Trump’s mission to end the war.
summary: US to mediate Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi next week, Witkoff says.
author: The Hill

title: Stevens explains rationale for endorsing Rogers over El-Sayed
content: Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) explained her decision to endorse former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s contested Senate race. Stevens cited campaign ads and other factors as part of her rationale. She stated that after concluding El-Sayed was not fit to serve in the United States Senate, she had to consider the alternative candidate.
summary: Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) shared her rationale for her recent decision to endorse former Rep.
author: The Hill

title: No Pro-Coal Candidates in Navajo Nation Presidential Election
content:
For the first time in decades, there is no pro‑coal candidate for Navajo Nation president.  

Coal has long been an important part of the economy, but voter sentiment is changing.
summary: For the first time in decades, the Navajo Nation presidential election has no pro-coal candidate. Voter sentiment is changing, as coal has been an important part of the economy.
author: NPR Politics

title: Red gold saffron harvested in Pampore, Jammu and Kashmir
content:
Kashmiri saffron is one of the world’s most expensive spices.

It is primarily cultivated in the Pampore region of Jammu and Kashmir in India. Often referred to as “red gold” because of its high value, saffron is prized for its rich aroma, distinctive flavour and quality.
summary: Kashmiri saffron is one of the world’s most expensive spices. It is primarily cultivated in the Pampore region of Jammu and Kashmir, India, and is referred to as ‘red gold’ because of its high value, prized for its rich aroma, distinctive flavour and quality.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Cervical cancer cases and deaths projected to rise by 20.2% and 39.3% by 2050
content: A modeling study published in Nature Medicine projects that global cervical cancer cases could increase by 20.2% and deaths by 39.3% by 2050. The analysis indicates that the disease burden will remain unevenly distributed, with the highest incidence and mortality rates concentrated in sub‑Saharan Africa.
summary: Cervical cancer cases and deaths projected to rise by 20.2% and 39.3% by 2050.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Plant compound may help overcome cancer drug resistance, study shows
content: A study by researchers at the Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center reports that a natural plant compound may help overcome a built‑in defense that allows many cancers to resist a class of drugs designed to restore normal gene activity. The compound could potentially counteract this resistance mechanism.
summary: A natural plant compound may help overcome a built-in defense that allows many cancers to resist a class of drugs designed to restore normal gene activity. The study was conducted by researchers at the Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center.
author: Medical Xpress

title: AI heart scan measurements better predict patient survival than clinician readings
content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) measurements of heart function derived from MRI scans show a stronger correlation with patient survival than measurements made by clinicians. The findings suggest that AI could serve as a useful first‑line method for assessing heart function.

The study was led by researchers at City St George's, University of London and University College London. It was published in The Lancet Digital Health.
summary: AI measurements of heart function from MRI scans are more strongly linked to patient survival than clinician measurements. The research, led by City St George's, University of London and University College London, was published in The Lancet Digital Health.
author: Medical Xpress

title: New study finds nurses overlooked in One Health movement
content: A new paper argues that nurses are among the most vital components of the health care workforce, yet their contributions remain largely overlooked. The study examines nurses’ role within the expanding “One Health” movement, which seeks to link human, animal and environmental health.
summary: A new paper argues that nurses are one of the most important parts of the health care workforce. However, their contribution is overlooked in the growing "One Health" movement that connects human, animal and environmental health.
author: Medical Xpress

title: SGLT2 Inhibitors Benefit Adults 80+ with Chronic Kidney Disease
content: A study presented at Kidney Week, the American Society of Nephrology’s annual meeting in Denver from Oct. 21‑25, found that SGLT2 inhibitors provide significant benefits for adults aged 80 and older with chronic kidney disease.
summary: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors show significant benefits for adults aged 80 years and older with chronic kidney disease. The study was presented at Kidney Week, the annual meeting of the American Society of Nephrology, held from Oct. 21 to 25 in Denver.
author: Medical Xpress

title: 60% of Australians Eat Raw Fish, Food Safety Council Warns Ahead of Food Safety Week
content: Ahead of Australian Food Safety Week, Nov. 7 to 14, 2026, with the theme "Raw food know the risk," the Food Safety Information Council has released new research showing 60% of Aussies consume raw fish or seafood, and 17% do so at least once a week.
summary: The Food Safety Information Council released new research ahead of Australian Food Safety Week, Nov. 7 to 14, 2026, showing that 60% of Aussies consume raw fish or seafood. The study also found that 17% of Aussies eat raw fish or seafood at least once a week.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Toddler snacks pulled from Costco, Target, Walmart and other stores over choking danger
content:
Toddler snacks have been removed from Costco, Target, Walmart and other retailers after a federal health warning.  

Parents and caregivers are urged to stop serving Once Upon a Farm Tractor Wheels toddler bars immediately, as federal health officials warn the product could cause deadly choking.
summary: Parents and caregivers should stop serving Once Upon a Farm Tractor Wheels toddler bars right away because they could cause deadly choking, federal health officials warn.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Queen's University Belfast students find Neptune's elusive Trojan asteroids
content: An international team led by researchers at Queen's University Belfast has identified Neptune's elusive Trojan asteroids, resolving a long-standing astronomical mystery. While telescope observations beginning in 1906 revealed "Trojan" and "Greek" populations leading and trailing Jupiter, similar families were later found orbiting Saturn and Uranus. Despite these discoveries, astronomers had not previously confirmed the existence of such asteroids around Neptune.
summary: An international team led by researchers at Queen's University Belfast discovered Neptune's Trojan asteroids, a population that had eluded astronomers for decades. This finding resolves the long-standing mystery of Neptune's missing Trojan families, which were previously known only around Jupiter, Saturn, and Uranus.
author: Phys.org

title: UK storm surges shaped by global climate patterns, Cambridge study finds
content: New research led by Cambridge University indicates that the specific location of storm surges along the U.K. coastline is determined by global climate patterns. These patterns extend across the Atlantic and Arctic regions, as well as areas even further afield, highlighting the far-flung connections between local coastal events and broader climate systems.
summary: New research led by Cambridge University shows that where a storm surge strikes along the UK coastline is decided by global climate patterns in the Atlantic, Arctic, and other regions. The study highlights that these patterns influence the surge location.
author: Phys.org

title: Analysis Links Square Chinese Characters to Linguistic, Technological, Cultural Factors
content: A new historical analysis published in the International Journal of Arts and Technology challenges prevailing views on the development of square Chinese characters. The study argues that these distinctive shapes emerged from interacting linguistic, technological, and cultural factors, rather than a single cause.
summary: A new historical analysis published in the International Journal of Arts and Technology challenges the received wisdom about why Chinese characters developed their distinctive square shapes. The study argues that the shape resulted from interacting linguistic, technological and cultural factors rather than a single cause.
author: Phys.org

title: PLOS Climate study finds tropical forests face shifting rainfall and extreme heat
content: A new study published in PLOS Climate shows that tropical regions previously considered safe from climate change are experiencing notable shifts in rainfall patterns and extreme temperature events. The paper, titled “Shifting climate in Caribbean tropical forests: Long‑term trends at La Selva (Costa Rica) and El Verde (Puerto Rico),” documents these significant changes in the Caribbean’s tropical forests.
summary: A new study finds that tropical areas often thought to be safe from climate change are experiencing significant changes in rainfall and extreme temperature events. The paper, titled "Shifting climate in Caribbean tropical forests: Long-term trends at La Selva (Costa Rica) and El Verde (Puerto Rico)," is published in PLOS Climate.
author: Phys.org

title: Ceres' Water Ice Masks Massive Surface Salt Deposits
content: The dwarf planet Ceres is described as one of the most overlooked objects in the solar system, largely because it is considered an "asteroid" despite sharing a dwarf planet designation with Pluto. Ceres resides in the main asteroid belt, where it stands as the largest object. Additionally, the dwarf planet accounts for between 25% and 30% of the total mass of the belt.
summary: Ceres, the largest object in the main asteroid belt, has water ice that can mask massive surface salt deposits. It accounts for between 25% and 30% of the belt's total mass.
author: Phys.org

title: Canadians Achieve Highest 2025 Federal Election Turnout Since 1993
content:
In the 2025 federal election, Canadians turned out to vote at the highest rate since 1993.  

Analysts typically explain variations in turnout by examining the national election campaign, noting how close the race was and what appeared to be at stake.
summary: In the 2025 federal election, Canadians voted at the highest rate since 1993. Explanations for turnout typically focus on the national campaign, such as race closeness and perceived stakes.
author: Phys.org

title: WorkOS reports security breach
content:
WorkOS has notified clients of a data security incident detected on October 30, 2026, at 16:39 UTC. The company identified anomalous traffic to an internal business system, with evidence suggesting the attack was driven by ARTEX, an AI-assisted autonomous penetration testing framework, from IP addresses in Hong Kong and China. The unauthorized actor accessed an internal API utilized by sales and marketing tools, which provided entry to Salesforce and Snowflake instances.

The compromised data includes business contact information, account and commercial details, aggregated product usage metrics, marketing contacts, and support tickets. Specific CRM information affected comprises names, email addresses, phone numbers, and company mailing addresses for WorkOS customers. WorkOS stated there is no evidence that application data or production services were accessed or impacted, indicating the incident was localized to CRM and customer support data. The company noted that the breach notification has not yet been posted on its website or Trust center.
summary: It's not on their website or Trust center yet, but we received the following breach notification from WorkOS: We are writing to notify you of a data security incident that we detected on October 30, 2026 and are continuing to investigate. We value your trust and want to keep you informed while our investigation continues.
author: Hacker News

title: User asks for contact to Cuyahoga Amateur Radio Club about removing radio gear
content:
