title: BMW to launch urban driver‑assist system in 2027
content:
BMW announced that it will expand its navigation‑guided, partially automated driving capabilities into urban environments beginning in 2027. The first rollout will occur in Germany, with other markets to follow.  

The new Level 2 system will use the vehicle’s built‑in GPS navigation to steer, accelerate, and decelerate on both highways and city streets. In town, it can assist with lane changes, turns, yielding to other vehicles, and navigating roundabouts. Drivers must keep their eyes on the road and remain ready to take over at any moment.
summary: BMW to launch urban driver‑assist system in 2027.
author: The Verge

title: Google discovers 1.3 million Videostrong devices used as botnet
content:
Google announced that its Android manufacturing partner, Shenzhen-based Videostrong Technology Co., secretly embedded a backdoor in 1.3 million Android TV devices to create a botnet. The company stated that these infected devices were used without owners’ knowledge for malicious activities, including ad fraud, data exfiltration, and routing unauthorized network traffic. Google characterized the backdoor and botnet as intentionally developed and operated for financial gain.

In response, Google dismantled the backdoor and cut ties with Videostrong. The manufacturer has been banned from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software for them.
summary: A current Videostrong Android TV device. Google says one of its Android manufacturing partners secretly built a backdoor in 1.3 million devices and turned them into a botnet.
author: The Verge

title: Meta to End Quest 2 OS Updates in 2027
content:
Meta has announced that it will release the final operating system update for its Quest 2 and Quest Pro virtual reality headsets by March 2027. This concluding update, designated as version 213, marks the end of major software support for these devices. Following this milestone, the company stated it will continue to provide security patches and critical bug fixes until the end of 2027. Additionally, developers will be able to submit applications compatible with the Quest 2 and Quest Pro through December 2027.

The announcement positions the Quest 3 and 3S as the new baseline for Meta’s VR gaming ecosystem. Meta is making this transition in anticipation of its upcoming VR Glasses, which are scheduled to launch in the spring of 2027. The company noted that the Quest 2 and Quest Pro have laid the foundation for its current hardware lineup.
summary: Meta will release the last OS update for its Quest 2 and Quest Pro VR headsets by March 2027, with v213 as the final version. After that, Meta will ship security patches and critical bug fixes through the end of 2027, and apps can be submitted through December 2027.
author: The Verge

title: Apple posts record $57.58 billion iPhone revenue in Q4 despite no standard model
content:
Apple reported a record‑breaking fourth‑quarter iPhone revenue of $57.58 billion, a 17 percent increase over the same period last year, according to its earnings release posted on Monday. The company achieved the jump even though it did not introduce a new standard iPhone model during its latest refresh.

The growth followed the September launch of the iPhone 18 lineup, which featured the pricier iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max models. Apple also raised prices on its older iPhone models at the same time. In addition, the company unveiled its first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, but preorder sales for that device were not included in the reported earnings.
summary: Apple reported $57.58 billion in iPhone revenue for the fourth quarter, a 17 percent increase from a year earlier. The rise followed the September launch of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, price hikes on older models, and the exclusion of iPhone Duo pre‑order sales from the report.
author: The Verge

title: Apple CEO says no timeline for resolving iPhone Duo supply shortage
content:
Apple CEO John Ternus said the company has no timeline for when supply constraints on the iPhone Duo could lift. In an interview with Reuters, he explained that Apple is working hard to get the device to as many customers as quickly as possible, but the company cannot predict when supply and demand will be in balance.

Apple launched its first foldable iPhone Duo last month for $1,999. The phone features a 5.4‑inch outer display and a 7.6‑inch inner screen. Pre‑orders sold out quickly, and some shipments are expected to arrive in 2027. A limited number of Duo models were also available in‑store at launch.
summary: Apple CEO says no timeline for resolving iPhone Duo supply shortage.
author: The Verge

title: China aims to land astronauts on Moon within three years
content:
China has announced that it intends to land astronauts on the Moon within the next three years. The statement came from Chinese space officials during the Seventh Manned Spaceflight Conference in Beijing, where they outlined the nation’s most detailed public plans for a series of missions that would culminate in a crewed lunar landing “before 2030.”

Chief designer for the lunar exploration program, Wang Xiang, was among the officials who presented the roadmap. The plan calls for a lunar‑orbit rendezvous, a technique used by NASA during the Apollo program of the 1960s and early 1970s. 

Because China does not yet have a launch vehicle as powerful as the Saturn V, the crew and the lunar lander will be launched separately to the Moon.
summary: China aims to land astronauts on Moon within three years.
author: Ars Technica

title: Anthropic adds Claude rule to block game cloning, but AI copying surge continues
content: Last week, Anthropic introduced a new system prompt designed to stop its Claude models from re-creating specific, existing video games. While that move could help shield Anthropic from some liability, it's unlikely to slow much of the massive wave of AI-assisted game porting and copying that has emerged in recent months. A social media user and AI decompilation enthusiast going by the name "chasm" was among the first to note the prompt change late last week, saying a new rule seemed to be added to the Claude Code prompt on or around October 27. That rule—included in a json file under the name "tengu_heron_brook"—reads as follows: Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original. XDA later independently verified that the new rule appears in version 2.1.314 of the Claude Code binary, which was released on October 30. XDA also reported that the "tengu_heron_brook" rule had been used for other purposes in earlier versions and that the Claude Opus 5.5 model specifically seemed to have its own distinct and independent instructions restricting game recreations as part of its system prompt bundle. Read full article Comments
summary: Last week, Anthropic introduced a new system prompt designed to stop its Claude models from re-creating specific, existing video games. While that move could help shield Anthropic from some liability, it's unlikely to slow much of the massive wave of AI-assisted game porting and copying that has emerged in recent months.
author: Ars Technica

title: Apple plans $1,000 home robot for FaceTime and light control, targeting 2027
content: Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room. People who worked on Apple’s robotic projects told The Information that the AI-driven home robot, code-named J595, could be named HomeView Ultra in line with Apple’s new HomeView stationary smart display. The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028. The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project. The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies. Read full article Comments
summary: Apple plans $1,000 home robot for FaceTime and light control, targeting 2027.
author: Ars Technica

title: Nature study finds common measures of cognitive reappraisal lack agreement
content: It's widely acknowledged that it's nearly impossible to publish negative results in scientific journals. "We didn't see anything" is a much harder sell than finding that a hypothesis is clearly right. Findings of no effect tend to either be shuffled off to low-profile journals or left behind as unpublished lab lore. The high-profile journal Nature, however, made a notable exception this week, publishing a study that tells us that a bunch of methods we have been using to try to measure a key emotional ability don't seem to be measuring the same thing. The results mean that we don't have a good way to measure the impact of a concept that is the basis of a key method in therapy. Inconsistencies One of the most successful forms of therapy is cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT. In part, CBT is based on getting people to step back and engage in "cognitive reappraisal." This requires people to think over a situation that has caused a negative emotional response and find ways to reinterpret it so that it has less impact on them. The ability to engage in this process has been linked to emotional resilience. Read full article Comments
summary: A study published in Nature reports that several methods used to assess a key emotional ability do not converge on the same construct. The findings suggest there is currently no reliable way to measure the impact of cognitive reappraisal, a process central to cognitive behavioral therapy.
author: Ars Technica

title: Google adds Zelda Easter egg that mimics 1998 search layout
content: The year was 1998. Britney Spears topped the charts, Bill Clinton was impeached, and a couple of little websites called Google and Ars Technica came online. It was also the year Nintendo released The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on the Nintendo 64. Google, which has come to dominate the Internet (Ars is still working on that), is celebrating the imminent release of the Ocarina of Time remaster by temporarily transporting us back to that storied year with a search Easter egg. To access the Google time machine, you just have to search for either "Zelda" or "Ocarina of Time." Google will load the standard 2026 results page, but you'll see an animated Master Sword in the lower right corner. It appears on both mobile and desktop—just click the sword and enjoy the show. After a little time-skipping animation and a Link shout (you know the one), you'll swear it's 1998 again. The search page is transformed into a simple list of blue links with retro Google branding. This is particularly apt given the time-shifting mechanics in Ocarina of Time. Read full article Comments
summary: Google adds Zelda Easter egg that mimics 1998 search layout.
author: Ars Technica

title: Third US bird flu death linked to infected dairy farm in Washington
content:
A Washington state resident died from avian influenza after being exposed at an infected dairy farm, state health officials said Sunday. The death is the third confirmed human bird‑flu fatality in the United States since a highly pathogenic H5 strain moved from wild migratory birds to dairy cattle, a jump first reported in March 2024.

The individual, a Yakima County resident, had underlying health conditions that may have increased vulnerability to the infection. County officials noted the person was severely ill and hospitalized on Friday before succumbing to the illness. Officials declined to release the person’s name, gender or age, citing family privacy.

Yakima Health District health officer Dave Atteberry expressed condolences and emphasized that avian influenza can cause severe illness in people with underlying conditions, but added that the overall risk to the general public remains low.
summary: Third US bird flu death linked to infected dairy farm in Washington.
author: Ars Technica

title: Snap settles lawsuit alleging platform fuels teen depression, eating disorders
content: Snap has settled a lawsuit that accused the platform of contributing to teen depression and eating disorders. The plaintiffs said they began using YouTube as early as age 3 and other social‑media services around age 9, developing compulsive usage habits they linked to features such as autoplay and infinite scrolling.
summary: Snap settled a lawsuit that accused its platform of contributing to teen depression and eating disorders. Plaintiffs said they began using YouTube at age 3 and other social media around age 9, developing compulsive usage habits they linked to features such as autoplay and infinite scrolling.

title: NY Times sues Brave for scraping content and giving it to Anthropic, Perplexity
content: The New York Times and additional media outlets have filed lawsuits against privacy‑focused web browser Brave, alleging that the company scraped copyrighted content from their publications and distributed it to Brave’s customers, including AI services such as Anthropic and Perplexity. The suits claim the scraping and distribution were unlawful.
summary: The New York Times is suing privacy-focused web browser company Brave for allegedly scraping its copyrighted content. The lawsuit says Brave unlawfully distributed the scraped material to its customers, including Anthropic and Perplexity.

title: Anthropic warns it is near RSI, a self‑building AI capability
content: RSI is the point at which AI grows so good at training itself that it spawns a dramatic acceleration of AI capabilities. To the AI doomers, RSI represents the cataclysm from which there is no return.
summary: Anthropic warned that it is very close to achieving RSI capability, also known as self‑building AI. RSI is defined as a point where AI can train itself, leading to a rapid acceleration of AI capabilities that some view as a catastrophic, irreversible event.

content: Londoners dressed as medieval knights took part in a Halloween jousting event, racing into battle on electric bikes. The spectacle attracted hundreds of spectators, offering a modern, electric‑bike twist on the traditional medieval sport.

content: Serbia is marking the two‑year anniversary of the Novi Sad railway station collapse, remembering the 16 people who died. Student leaders in power have pledged to pursue justice for the victims and to seek accountability for alleged corruption linked to the tragedy.
summary: Serbia marks two years since the Novi Sad railway station collapse. Students in power have pledged justice for the 16 victims and accountability for alleged corruption.

content: Ukraine’s Skyfall reports that its “Stargate” drone evacuated two wounded soldiers from the front line, flying a 15 km route each way at speeds of up to 105 km/h.

title: Efrat Shapira expects President Herzog to urge rival camps to form coalition
content: Erin Ogunkeye is pleased to welcome Efrat Shapira Rosenberg, Israeli Radio/TV Host, Columnist, Podcaster and Educator. Following a deadlocked Israeli election, “everyone is saying who they’re not going to sit with, but no one is actually saying who they will sit with.” As President Isaac Herzog prepares to consult parliamentary factions over the formation of a new coalition, the impasse reveals tensions that extend beyond the familiar confrontation between Benjamin Netanyahu and his political opponents. According to Shapira, co-host of the highly popular Israeli politics podcast Miflaget Hamakshavot, the divisions are equally pronounced within the opposition bloc supporting Gadi Eisenkot.
summary: Efrat Shapira Rosenberg, an Israeli radio/TV host, columnist, podcaster and educator, said President Isaac Herzog is preparing to consult parliamentary factions on forming a new coalition after a deadlocked election. She noted the impasse reveals divisions not only between Benjamin Netanyahu and his opponents but also within the opposition bloc supporting Gadi Eisenkot.
author: France 24

title: Trump’s Loyal Supporters Turning Against Him as Approval Hits 32%
content:
The article raises the question of whether Donald Trump is losing the support of the coalition that helped him return to the White House. Just one day before the mid‑term elections, his approval rating is reported at 32 %, one of the lowest figures recorded at that point in a presidency.

The piece notes that discontent is spreading beyond Democratic voters. Some of Trump’s most loyal Republican and MAGA supporters are reportedly torn between political loyalty and economic reality. Factors cited include the war in Iran, rising costs linked to the Strait of Hormuz blockade, unfulfilled “America First” promises, and the Epstein files scandal, all of which are said to widen the rift between the president and his electoral base.

The article concludes by asking whether Trump can regain control of the diverse MAGA coalition. France 24 journalist Stella Elgersma interviewed MAGA and Republican experts to examine how the movement has evolved, what its supporters want, and what is driving their discontent. The full documentary is available on YouTube at https://youtu.be/XkehRG77itY?Si=iOfIl0PwrgyX-j0X.
summary: Is Trump losing the support of the very coalition that brought him back to power? Just one day before the midterm elections, Trump's approval rating stands at 32%, one of the lowest ever recorded at this stage of a presidency.
author: France 24

title: Questions raised about president’s response if midterms defeat his party
content:
The upcoming US Midterm elections raise questions about the extent to which the president will influence outcomes if they do not favor his party. The text highlights campaign promises contingent on Republican victories and notes that the US Justice Department has already intervened in specific races, prompting inquiries about the White House’s potential impact on the election results.

Additionally, the article examines the state of ballot counting procedures and contrasts the current political landscape with the period following the president’s “stop the steal” rhetoric, which preceded the January 6, 2021, storming of the US Capitol. These issues frame a broader assessment of the state of US democracy ahead of the Tuesday vote.
summary: The piece asks how far the president of the United States might press if Tuesday’s midterm elections do not favor his party. It also questions the role of campaign promises, Justice Department involvement, ballot counting and changes since the “stop the steal” rhetoric and the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack.
author: France 24

title: EU calls fridge cyberattacks deliberate attempt to disrupt food supply
content:
Grocery stores across at least eight EU countries, from Sweden to Portugal, were hit on Monday by a suspected cyberattack that targeted freezer systems. The European Union described the incident as a deliberate attempt to disrupt the bloc’s food chain. Supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg and the Netherlands were among those affected, and the attack followed a cyber‑incident three weeks earlier that disrupted French grocery stores.

The temperature rise in the refrigerators forced food retailers to discard produce that had spoiled or was at risk of spoiling. The report was delivered by FRANCE 24’s Dave Keating from Brussels.
summary: EU calls fridge cyberattacks deliberate attempt to disrupt food supply.
author: France 24

title: The Long Hull: Karl Bushby reflects on perseverance & 'best of humanity' on his 28-year journey home
content: “They say it takes a village. In this case, it took a world.” After 28 years and some 50,000 kilometres, British explorer and adventurer Karl Bushby has returned to his hometown of Hull, completing an extraordinary life journey across four continents that illustrates not only the limits of human endurance, but also the intricate relationship between individual determination, geopolitical constraints and a world of humanity. Speaking to France 24's François Picard shortly after his emotional homecoming, Bushby reflects on an undertaking that resembles a modern-day Odyssey, although the defining obstacles were often more geopolitical than mythological.
summary: The Long Hull: Karl Bushby reflects on perseverance & 'best of humanity' on his 28-year journey home.
author: France 24

content: Uganda has begun drawing down its troops from the peacekeeping mission in Somalia, a move announced in tonight’s edition and occurring just days after the United Nations concluded its political mission in the country. In related regional news, upcoming municipal elections in South Africa may solidify growing political fragmentation, while Chad is experiencing a drought that could be its worst in more than four decades.
summary: Uganda is beginning to draw down its troops from the peacekeeping mission in Somalia. The drawdown comes just days after the UN ends its political mission in Somalia.

title: Trump’s “no more wars” pledge contrasts with US involvement in multiple global conflicts
content:
Donald Trump pledged an “America First” foreign policy and vowed to keep the United States out of foreign wars.  

Since returning to the White House, his administration has become deeply involved in a range of international conflicts. The record includes U.S. engagement in the war in Ukraine, threats to Greenland and Canada, intervention in Venezuela, and a shifting approach to the Middle East and the war with Iran.  

Vedika Bahl examines this foreign‑policy trajectory, highlighting how the administration’s actions contrast with the earlier promise of non‑intervention.
summary: Donald Trump promised an “America First” foreign policy and pledged to keep the US out of foreign wars. But since returning to the White House, his administration has been deeply involved in conflicts around the world.
author: France 24

title: Iliana Yotova wins Bulgaria's presidential election, vows to be president of peace
content: Iliana Yotova won the presidential election in Bulgaria, pledging to serve as a “president of peace.” Her campaign highlighted the country’s deep divisions over the war in Ukraine and over drone attacks in the Black Sea.
summary: Iliana Yotova won the presidential election in Bulgaria, promising to be a "president of peace." The campaign revealed deep divisions among Bulgarians over the war in Ukraine and drone attacks in the Black Sea.

content: Karl Bushby, a British man, has returned to the UK after a 28‑year journey covering 50,000 km without transport. He began in Chile and crossed the Americas, Russia, Central Asia and Europe, almost entirely on foot.
summary: Karl Bushby, a British man, has returned to the UK after walking 50,000 km over 28 years. He began in Chile and crossed the Americas, Russia, Central Asia and Europe almost entirely on foot.

title: Germany's Chancellor Merz Calls for Reunified Korea During Visit
content: During a recent visit, German Chancellor Olaf Merz called for a reunified Korea, noting that Germany, like Korea, was once divided by rival political systems and a heavily fortified border. The report adds that the prospect of Korean unity appears faint.
summary: Germany, like Korea, was once divided by rival political systems and a fortified border. Chancellor Merz called for a reunified Korea during his recent visit, but the prospect seems faint.

title: Question raised about Trump's possible Iran plans after US midterms
content: The U.S. midterm elections could either open a window for renewed diplomacy with Iran or trigger a new military escalation. Deutsche Welle interviewed analysts who identified eight factors that could tip the balance toward war or peace in the post‑midterm period.

title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to block over 20,000 California midterm ballots
content:
The Trump administration has petitioned the U.S. Supreme Court to block more than 20,000 California mid‑term ballots, citing allegations that the ballots contain non‑U.S. citizens.  

Multiple courts and independent analyses have rejected those allegations, finding no evidence that the ballots were ineligible.

title: US says South Africa, Rwanda violating AGOA rules, to be removed from duty‑free trade
content: The Trump administration announced that South Africa and Rwanda are violating the rules of the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), a key U.S. free‑trade program with sub‑Saharan Africa. As a result, the United States will remove both countries from the AGOA duty‑free trade initiative.
summary: The Trump administration said South Africa and Rwanda are breaking the rules of the AGOA free trade initiative. The United States will drop them from the duty‑free trade program.

title: Investigative report reveals Mexican women soldiers ordered into officers' bedrooms
content: An investigative report by Zorayda Gallegos reveals that in Mexico’s armed forces, orders from superiors are expected to be obeyed without question. Gallegos found that for many women in uniform, such orders can involve being asked to step into an officer’s bedroom.
summary: In Mexico’s armed forces, orders from superiors are expected to be obeyed without question. Investigative journalist Zorayda Gallegos found that many women in uniform are ordered to step into an officer’s bedroom.

title: UNESCO report finds six in seven journalist murders go unpunished, impunity rises
content: UNESCO’s latest report finds that six of every seven journalist murders remain unpunished, marking the first rise in global impunity for such killings in more than a decade. The study also highlights the growing use of drones as an emerging threat to reporters operating in conflict zones.
summary: The UNESCO report says six of seven journalist murders go unpunished, marking a rise in global impunity for the first time in more than a decade. It also warns that the growing use of drones is an emerging threat for reporters in conflict zones.

title: WHO chief warns northern Ethiopia violence threatens health system
content: The head of the World Health Organization warned that violence in northern Ethiopia is pushing the health system to the brink. On Monday, the WHO chief called for greater protection for civilians caught in the conflict after deadly drone strikes occurred over the past weekend.
summary: The WHO chief warned that violence in northern Ethiopia is pushing the health system to the brink. He called on Monday for greater protection for civilians after deadly drone strikes over the weekend.

title: WFP delivers hot meals to over 400 Oleshky evacuees amid ceasefire
content: The UN World Food Programme is delivering hot meals to more than 400 evacuees who left the Russian‑occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region during a brief local ceasefire. At the same time, the United Nations is urging the restoration of electricity in the area before winter arrives.

title: Andy Burnham rejects “open borders” label while discussing Labour immigration reform
content:
Andy Burnham, speaking on the campaign trail in Makerfield, offered a preview of his position on Labour’s immigration‑reform proposals. He noted that the plans have been criticised by the party’s left as unfair and described by the right as electorally necessary. When asked about Reform’s accusation that he favours “open borders” – a label first used by Nigel Farage – the former Manchester mayor called the charge “ridiculous” and defended his stance.

The article also notes that the prime minister wants to link Shabana Mahmood’s hard‑line border approach to a broader recognition of migration’s value, suggesting Burnham may need to articulate his conviction more forcefully.

content:
Andy Burnham will launch a “structured dialogue” on Britain’s role in slavery at the Commonwealth heads‑of‑government summit (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda.  

Downing Street said the prime minister will ask countries affected by Britain’s involvement in slavery to help shape an expected formal apology, stressing that their input is indispensable for crafting a lasting message.  

The summit begins on Tuesday, and No 10 confirmed that Burnham will use the event to explore what form the apology might take.

title: Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen calls historic chance to oust Netanyahu
content:
The leader of Israel’s main Palestinian coalition, Yousef Jabareen, said the country faces a “historic” opportunity to change direction after his bloc secured a record number of seats in the Knesset. Jabareen, who heads the Joint List, noted that his coalition now holds the balance of power following Tuesday’s elections.

He added that he is prepared to join forces with the opposition “Change” bloc to oust Benjamin Netanyahu and his far‑right coalition and to wrest control of the Knesset.

title: Poll: Majority of Israelis say settlements policy must change to avoid further sanctions
content:
A recent poll of Israelis found that a majority believe the country’s settlements policy should be altered to prevent further sanctions. The survey, released after the general election, indicates that many voters see a link between settlement actions and international punitive measures.

The poll also revealed that the United Kingdom’s decision to impose a trade ban on goods from illegal settlements was not a decisive factor in how Israelis voted. Respondents said the ban did not influence their electoral choices.

The UK’s ban, announced by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband in September, drew fierce criticism. Some commentators argued that the sanctions could push Israeli voters toward supporting Benjamin Netanyahu, but the poll suggests that this concern did not shape the election outcome.
summary: A new poll shows most Israelis believe Israel's settlements policy should be altered to prevent additional sanctions. The survey found the UK government's trade ban on goods from illegal settlements was not a decisive factor in how Israelis voted in their general election.

title: Brent crude falls to $105.55, lowest in over two weeks amid Iran war hopes
content: Brent crude fell more than 6 % on Monday, reaching $105.55 a barrel, the lowest price since 16 October and the lowest level in more than two weeks. The decline came as new hopes emerged of a breakthrough that could end the war involving Iran. The drop in oil prices lifted airline‑company shares and reduced government borrowing costs.
summary: Brent crude falls to $105.55, lowest in over two weeks amid Iran war hopes.

title: French pupils block schools again as government braces for further protests
content: Dozens of high schools across France were blockaded again on Monday as the government prepared for a tense week of protests over school conditions and the high cost of living. Unions have scheduled a nationwide strike for Thursday, prompting a minister’s warning that the cumulative weeks without lessons could jeopardise pupils’ school year and final exams. The renewed blockades reflect growing concern that extended disruptions may put exams at risk.
summary: Dozens of high schools across France were blockaded again on Monday as unions prepared a nationwide strike on Thursday. A minister warned that weeks without lessons are putting pupils’ exams at risk.

title: EU condemns cyber‑attack that raised supermarket fridge temperatures in seven countries
content: After a second apparent cyber-attack in as many weeks, we examine possible culprits and their motives Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries have malfunctioned, their thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C (122F). The EU has condemned what it said was “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.
summary: Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries malfunctioned after a suspected cyber‑attack that remotely raised thermostats to as high as 50 °C. The EU said the incident was a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain and undermine consumer confidence.

title: Scientists find fossilized red blood cells and heme in 115‑million‑year‑old Aratasaurus bone
content:
Scientists report finding what appear to be fossilised red blood cells in the hind‑leg bone of a small carnivorous dinosaur named Aratasaurus. The specimen lived in present‑day north‑eastern Brazil about 115 million years ago.  

Chemical analyses detected heme, the organic component of haemoglobin that transports oxygen, indicating traces of the molecule that gave the dinosaur’s blood a red colour. The researchers describe the finding as evidence of preserved blood‑cell structures in the Jurassic‑period bone.
summary: Chemical tests on the hind‑leg bone of the small meat‑eating dinosaur Aratasaurus, which lived in what is now north‑eastern Brazil 115 million years ago, identified the presence of heme. The researchers say the analysis shows fossilised red blood cells in the bone.
author: Guardian World

title: NASA MRO Captures Color-Enhanced View of Ancient Rocky Hill on Mars
content:
NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) captured a color-enhanced image of an ancient, rocky hill in the Red Planet’s Southern Highlands, featured as the Space photo of the day for Nov. 2, 2026. The image, taken by the HiRISE camera, displays a rainbow-hued rocky plain that highlights the region's mineral-rich terrain. The MRO has been studying Mars’ surface, atmosphere, and climate since entering orbit in March 2006.

The image is not a natural-color representation of the Martian surface but has been color-enhanced to amplify slight color variations in the rocks. This scientific technique allows researchers to distinguish between different mineral compositions that would otherwise be difficult to identify in standard imagery. By enhancing these subtle differences, scientists can more effectively analyze the geological makeup of the area.

According to scientists analyzing the image, the blue- and green-toned rocks may contain minerals such as pyroxenes and olivine. Conversely, the yellow, orange, and red patches are believed to contain minerals formed by past interactions with liquid water. These distinct color signatures serve as visual indicators of the specific chemical processes that occurred in the region.

The analysis of these mineral contents helps researchers uncover the history preserved in Martian bedrock. The presence of certain minerals suggests that water flowed on Mars long ago, indicating potentially habitable conditions in the planet's past. Consequently, this striking image provides significant clues to Mars’ geological and environmental history beyond its aesthetic appeal.
summary: The HiRISE camera aboard the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter captured a color-enhanced image of an ancient rocky hill in Mars' Southern Highlands. Scientists use the enhanced colors to identify minerals like pyroxenes and olivine, which may indicate past interactions with liquid water.
author: Space.com

title: Expedition 1 Arrives at the International Space Station on Nov. 2, 2000
content:
On November 2, 2000, the International Space Station (ISS) welcomed its first long-term residents, marking the arrival of Expedition 1. The crew consisted of NASA astronaut Bill Shepherd and Russian cosmonauts Yuri Gidzenko and Sergei Krikalev. This mission differed from previous operations because the crew arrived via a Russian Soyuz spacecraft, which was the first Soyuz to dock with the station, rather than a Space Shuttle. While NASA had previously launched five one-week Space Shuttle missions to construct the station and deliver supplies, Expedition 1 established a continuous human presence by planning a four-and-a-half-month stay.

During their time aboard the ISS, the Expedition 1 crew unpacked supplies and installed new equipment, including the station’s first solar arrays. The mission concluded when the crew departed aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery, which simultaneously delivered the Expedition 2 crew to take their place. This transition ensured that the station remained continuously occupied, a status that has persisted for 26 years according to the source.

The arrival of Expedition 1 is significant as it demonstrated that the ISS could successfully support human crews living and working in orbit. Although the ISS was not the first space station, it has become the longest-running one. Since these initial pioneers, hundreds of astronauts from around the world have flown to and lived aboard the station. While NASA has indicated the station may be decommissioned in the coming years, the source notes that these early accomplishments remain a permanent part of spaceflight history.
summary: On Nov. 2, 2000, the International Space Station welcomed its first long-term residents: NASA astronaut Bill Shepherd and two Russian cosmonauts, Yuri Gidzenko and Sergei Krikalev.
author: Space.com

title: Alex Garland's Elden Ring Film Aimed at Becoming Hollywood's Goriest Fantasy
content: The expansive project has hype and money behind it – but how do you avoid it falling into the disappointment trap so many films end up stumbling into? If the history of failed Hollywood fantasy projects over the past 20 years has taught us anything, it is that transporting audiences to another world is only half the battle: you also have to give them a reason to spend several hours there. The Golden Compass diluted Philip Pullman’s theological bite, Warcraft thought that just explaining its world would make us care about it, and The Dark Tower compressed Stephen King’s sprawling mythology so ruthlessly that it scarcely left room for a story. All these films at one point had fans of the original source material quivering with anticipation at the prospect of seeing their beloved worlds on the big screen; all ended up disappointing. Which brings us to the forthcoming Alex Garland adaptation of the hugely popular high fantasy video game, Elden Ring. If there was ever a cinematic test of the phrase “too big to fail”, it is surely this. Elden Ring has sold more than 30m copies and is widely regarded as one of the greatest video games ever made. George RR Martin himself wrote the foundational mythology of warring demigods that underpins its gorgeous fantasy hellscape. And Garland as writer-director seems almost impossibly perfect: as the creative behind Dredd, Ex Machina and Annihilation, he has both the taste for beautiful nightmares and the geek credentials to deliver something extraordinary.
summary: The upcoming adaptation of the video game Elden Ring is positioned as a major cinematic project with significant financial backing and high expectations. Writer-director Alex Garland is helming the film, which is based on a game that has sold over 30 million copies and features foundational mythology written by George RR Martin.
author: Guardian Culture

title: ‘We both know how we feel about death and dying’: Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney on their brutally honest Parkinson’s drama
content:
Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney star in Onwards and Sideways, a BBC film set in Norfolk and directed by John Madden. The project, written by Paul Mayhew-Archer, who has Parkinson’s disease, follows a couple who bond over their respective diagnoses of the neurological condition. The actors noted that while the subject matter is devastating, the narrative is laced with humour.

Ahead of their first collaborative job, Ifans and Linney skipped the standard “chemistry read” to assess their compatibility. This decision was notable given the intense physical and emotional demands of their roles. In the film, Ifans’s character nearly throttles Linney during night terrors, while her character collapses in his arms after bankrupting herself through a gambling addiction. Both dramatic scenarios stem directly from the Parkinson’s disease affecting their characters.
summary: ‘We both know how we feel about death and dying’: Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney on their brutally honest Parkinson’s drama.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Mal Evans Says Meeting Elvis Was His Biggest Day With The Beatles
content:
Mal Evans, the former road manager for the Beatles, described his meeting with Elvis Presley as “the biggest day of all the years I have spent with the famous Beatles” in a memoir that has not been previously published. The book, which Evans intended to release with the band’s permission, offers various recollections from his time with the group.

Evans died in 1976 at the age of 40 following a shooting by Los Angeles police. The incident is believed to have been “suicide by cop” after he repeatedly pointed an air rifle at officers, an act attributed to his distress over the breakup of his marriage.
summary: Mal Evans Says Meeting Elvis Was His Biggest Day With The Beatles.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Writer explains why (500) Days of Summer is their feelgood movie
content: The writer continues a series about their most rewatched comfort films, noting that the movie in question holds special romantic meaning. The narrative is set in September 2009, when Barack Obama was settling into the White House, the global economy was cautiously recovering from the financial crisis, and Keisha had just left the Sugababes. At that moment, the writer was on a first date.

content:
After Guardian writers selected their Halloween picks, readers responded with films that send chills down their spines, including Never Let Me Go and The Truman Show.

One reader described the murder of a taxi driver as excruciating, noting a hanging at the end. The scene was shown in full, close‑up, and real time, and the condemned man’s last cigarette was smoked.

The audience’s unease was palpable. The piece was signed by Wiscot.

title: Taika Waititi Blasts Critics Over Klara and the Sun Box-Office Disaster
content: The Jojo Rabbit director blamed the dismal numbers for his film of Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel on ‘obsolete’ reviewers’ notices, adding that he works ‘for the people’ – whose Rotten Tomatoes ratings are much higher Taika Waititi has launched a furious broadside at “critics” following the disastrous commercial performance of Klara and the Sun, his new film adapted from a Kazuo Ishiguro novel. In a post on social media, Waititi wrote: “This Halloween, let’s spare a thought for those sad lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics.”
summary: Taika Waititi criticized reviewers after Klara and the Sun performed poorly at the box office. In a social media post, he urged empathy for artists who became critics.

title: Ashanti Reveals Bodysuit Incident and Plans to Re-Record 25-Year-Old Album
content:
Ashanti is preparing for her upcoming Australian tour, during which she discussed her marriage to Nelly, the enthusiasm of fans rushing the stage, and a secret skill she keeps private.  

She revealed that her debut album, Ashanti, will be re‑recorded as it turns 25 next year.  The singer said the new version will give her ownership of the masters and a clearer sonic quality while preserving the classic vibe that fans love.  She expressed excitement about the project and gratitude for the lasting impact of her early records.  

Ashanti also noted that “Foolish” is turning 25 and that she still enjoys performing in arenas, holding the mic and hearing audiences sing along.  She described that experience as a beautiful feeling and a blessing.
summary: Ashanti discussed her marriage to Nelly, fans rushing the stage, and a secret skill during an interview ahead of her Australian tour. She also announced she is re-recording her debut album, which turns 25 next year, to own her masters and give it a clearer sound.

title: Tomb Raider creators say game’s success had staff pulling up in sports cars
content: ‘Giving Lara Croft pistols meant we could show off her acrobatics. And when she goes to Peru, we threw in a T rex!’ I joined Core Design in the summer of 1994 and met Toby Gard, who showed me his concept sketches for Tomb Raider. title: London City Lionesses fall 2-1 to Manchester City
content:
London City Lionesses remain in third place in the Women’s Super League, holding a three-point lead over fourth-placed Tottenham. The team’s position has been bolstered by a poor start from Arsenal, who dropped points despite dominating their match against Villa. Although London City lost 2-1 to champions Manchester City in Bromley, their coach Eder Maestre stated that the result did not reflect the team’s performance, noting that Manchester City’s greater maturity and consistency gave them an edge.

The article highlights a potential future challenge for UEFA regarding club ownership. If London City Lionesses continue their upward trajectory and qualify for the Champions League, UEFA would need to address the scenario of two clubs owned by Michelle Kang—London City and OL Lyonnes—qualifying simultaneously. Maestre expressed frustration over the loss, emphasizing that his team deserved a better outcome against the more experienced Manchester City side.
summary: London City Lionesses fall 2-1 to Manchester City.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or celebration turns into anxiety‑filled hangover for Bayern Munich
content:
Bayern Munich’s celebration of Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or victory took a somber turn during their recent match against Borussia Dortmund. Prior to the game, the club held a guard of honor for the England captain, who had been awarded the prize two nights earlier. The pre-match atmosphere was festive, with Kane appearing on the stadium’s giant scoreboard holding the golden trophy and smiling, marking a significant milestone in his partnership with the club.

However, the anticipated victory lap did not materialize. Dortmund did not follow the expected script, resulting in a draw that left the defending champions level on points with the visitors at the top of the table. The outcome shifted the mood from the celebratory pre-game ceremony to a more anxious reality for Bayern Munich, as the competitive nature of the classic fixture ultimately overshadowed the individual accolade.
summary: Harry Kane's Ballon d’Or trophy was celebrated by Bayern Munich players, who welcomed him onto the pitch with a guard of honour. The party, however, turned into an anxiety‑filled hangover for the club.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Dazn Secures Exclusive Global Streaming Rights for 2029 Club World Cup
content:
Dazn has secured an exclusive option for the global streaming rights to the next men’s Club World Cup in 2029, a move that deepens its partnership with Fifa. The Saudi Arabia-backed streaming company previously came to Fifa’s aid before the inaugural 32-team Club World Cup in the United States last year.

At that time, Dazn agreed to pay $1 billion for the global rights to the 2025 tournament after many linear broadcasters and other streamers had declined to bid.
summary: Dazn has secured an exclusive option for global streaming rights to the 2029 men's Club World Cup, deepening its partnership with Fifa. The company previously paid $1 billion for global rights to the 2025 tournament after other broadcasters declined to bid.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Jack Grealish left out of Everton squad for Premier League trip to Newcastle
content:
Jack Grealish was omitted from Everton’s squad for the upcoming Premier League match against Newcastle on Monday, marking his third successive absence.  
The playmaker was dropped from the Carabao Cup win over Matthias Jaissle’s team last Thursday after missing training without permission in the build‑up to the fourth‑round tie.  
He had also been absent from the previous league defeat at Arsenal, where illness kept him out. Grealish left on Merseyside to work on his fitness as Everton prepare to host Newcastle.
summary: Jack Grealish is expected to miss his third consecutive Everton match as the team visits Newcastle in the Premier League. The 31-year-old was omitted from the previous Carabao Cup match for disciplinary reasons after missing training without permission.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Bucs win 16-0 vs Falcons with zero passing yards
content:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers completed a 16‑0 victory over the Atlanta Falcons on Sunday, a game in which the team recorded zero passing yards.  The Bucs attempted only three passes, all of which were incomplete, and Baker Mayfield was the only quarterback involved in the passing attack.

Mayfield’s three attempts marked the first time a Buccaneers team has gone a game without a single completed pass since the Buffalo Bills beat the New York Jets 16‑12 on 29 September 1974.  The game was played in a heavy downpour that prompted the Bucs to rely almost exclusively on their ground attack.

The rushing effort was the centerpiece of the win.  Tampa Bay carried the ball 56 times for 324 yards, the most rushing yards ever achieved by the franchise in a single game.  Bucky Irving rushed for 170 yards and a touchdown, while Kenneth Gainwell added 140 yards on the ground.

In the rain‑slick conditions, Mayfield’s role was largely limited to blocking for the running backs, and the Buccaneers’ success hinged on their dominant rushing performance.
summary: The Tampa Bay Buccaneers defeated the Atlanta Falcons 16-0, completing zero passes in the game. Bucky Irving rushed for 170 yards and a touchdown while Kenneth Gainwell added 140 yards, and the team amassed 324 rushing yards on 56 carries, the most in a single game in franchise history.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Asa Tribe barred from England Lions tour over Ebola concerns after Kenya trip
content:
Glamorgan opener Asa Tribe has been barred from joining the England Lions tour of the Caribbean after visiting Kenya, citing concerns over the recent Ebola outbreak in east Africa. The 22-year-old, who can represent his native Jersey until earning a senior England cap, played three List A games for the associate nation in Nairobi last month.

The entry ban was implemented by the St Kitts and Nevis government. Tribe was originally scheduled to travel from Kenya to join the England Lions squad in St Kitts and Nevis.
summary: Glamorgan opener Asa Tribe, 22, was barred from joining the England Lions Caribbean tour after playing List A games for Jersey in Nairobi, Kenya. The ban was imposed due to Ebola concerns by the St Kitts and Nevis government.
author: Guardian Sport

title: England’s early exit from Rugby League World Cup highlights need for systemic change
content:
English rugby league has called for systemic change, arguing that the national side must receive higher priority after an early exit from the Rugby League World Cup. The criticism highlights a perceived decline in the sport over the past eight to ten years.

Damning remarks about the state of English rugby league were first made by former Kangaroos coach Ricky Stuart almost two decades ago. Stuart delivered the comments after England’s men were beaten in the semi‑finals of the 2008 Rugby League World Cup, and his stance remains influential today.

England has failed to reach the last four for the first time, having not qualified from an arguably farcical group‑stage format. The result underscores the urgency of the reforms called for by the sport’s critics.
summary: Former Australia coach Ricky Stuart criticised England’s rugby league after the 2008 semi‑final loss, and his remarks still carry weight. England’s early exit from the Rugby League World Cup, the first time they failed to reach the last four, underscores a need for systemic change and a higher priority for the national side.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest F1 world champion at 20
content:
Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli made history this year by becoming Formula One’s youngest world champion at 20 years old, a record that also marked Italy’s first championship since Alberto Ascari in 1953. The story began before the 2026 season, when most of the F1 community believed Mercedes had the fastest car and George Russell was the favourite for the title. Antonelli, then a teenage teammate, was seen as a prodigious talent who would need further development after a challenging rookie season.

That consensus lasted only one race. By the sixth round, Antonelli had turned expectations on their head, establishing himself as a serious contender for the championship. Observers noted his strong performance in a car that dominated the first two‑thirds of the season, and praised his verve, aggressive skill, judgment, and moments of maturity that belied his age.

Antonelli’s triumph is notable not only for the record it set but for the manner in which he achieved it, drawing attention to his rapid growth and competitive spirit on the track.
summary: Kimi Antonelli, a 20‑year‑old Mercedes driver, won the Formula One World Championship in his second season. He became the youngest champion and Italy's first champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Republican candidates struggle for message beyond Trump in 2026 midterms
content: Republican candidates running in the 2026 midterm elections are reported to be having difficulty crafting a persuasive message that extends beyond loyalty to Donald Trump. The candidates also confront voter concerns about corruption, the economy and the president’s low approval rating as the election approaches.
summary: Republican candidates in the 2026 midterms have struggled to find a compelling message beyond loyalty to Donald Trump. They also face challenges regarding corruption, the economy, and low presidential approval ratings ahead of tomorrow's election.

title: El-Sayed raises $1.2M in four hours after Stevens backs Rogers
content:
Abdul El‑Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s Senate seat, raised $1.2 million in four hours.  
The surge followed former primary rival Rep. Haley Stevens endorsing Republican Mike Rogers for the vacant seat.
summary: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed raised $1.2 million in four hours after former primary rival Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers for the vacant Senate seat.

content: Two people were killed in a murder‑suicide outside the Amazon Fulfillment Center on Twin Mills Road in Virginia Beach, Virginia, police said. The incident occurred Sunday afternoon, around 2:30 p.m. on November 1, when the Virginia Beach Police Department’s Emergency Communications and Citizen Services received a reported shooting in the 1800 block.
summary: VIRGINIA BEACH, Va. (WAVY) — Two people are dead after a murder-suicide outside of the Amazon Fulfillment Center on Twin Mills Road in Virginia Beach, Va., Sunday afternoon, according to the Virginia Beach Police Department.

content: Vice President Vance is campaigning in New York and Ohio on Monday to rally Republican voters ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. His first stop is Rome, N.Y., where he will join GOP House candidate Anthony Constantino. The source notes that Constantino is running in a district that President Trump previously carried by a 21-point margin.

content: Google’s AI summary is reportedly cutting deeply into its own profits, raising questions about its impact. Meanwhile, First Dog on the Moon encourages readers to sign up for email updates on new cartoons and to visit the First Dog shop for merchandise and prints.

title: Europe could face colder weather as polar vortex weakens
content:
Disruption to winds above the Arctic threatens to alter weather patterns across parts of Europe in the coming weeks. The stratospheric polar vortex over the northern hemisphere is facing an unusually early weakening, a shift that normally would not occur until later in the season.

Forecast models indicate the vortex could weaken significantly over the next ten days, when it would typically be strengthening. A major sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) event is possible, which could influence weather patterns in the following weeks by increasing the likelihood of persistent areas of high pressure across the mid‑latitudes and colder conditions weeks later.
summary: Forecast models suggest the stratospheric polar vortex could weaken significantly over the next 10 days, an unusual early weakening. This could trigger a major sudden stratospheric warming event, increasing the likelihood of persistent high pressure areas and colder conditions in the mid-latitudes in the following weeks.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Greenpeace activists drop boulders to block industrial trawling in North Sea MPA
content:
Greenpeace activists have dropped boulders in the North Sea to prevent bottom trawling and protect porpoise populations. The action was aimed at snagging the drag nets of industrial trawlers operating in a marine protected area.

The stones were placed by crew aboard the Greenpeace ship Arctic Sunrise, creating an underwater barrier around the Southern North Sea marine protected area (MPA). The Southern North Sea MPA is the UK’s most bottom‑trawled protected area.
summary: Greenpeace activists on the ship Arctic Sunrise dropped giant stones in the North Sea to create an underwater barrier around the Southern North Sea marine protected area. The barrier is intended to deter industrial trawlers from bottom trawling in the UK's most bottom‑trawled MPA.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Narrow-headed ant nest stolen from Devon's Chudleigh Knighton Heath, England's last site
content:
A nest containing up to 5,000 of England’s rarest ant species was stolen from Chudleigh Knighton Heath nature reserve in south Devon, the conservation charity Devon Wildlife Trust (DWT) said. The nest, home to the narrow‑headed ant, was dug up and taken from the reserve, which is the last place in England where the species still exists.

DWT described the theft as “reckless” and said it sets back years of conservation work on the species. The loss underscores the vulnerability of the ant’s remaining population in the UK.
summary: A nest of up to 5,000 narrow-headed ants was dug up and taken from Chudleigh Knighton Heath nature reserve in south Devon. Devon Wildlife Trust said the reckless theft sets back years of conservation work and removes the species from England’s last surviving location.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Republican Support Wanes in Dare County as Flooding Response Criticized
content: At more than $52m, the race has become the most expensive in US history, but residents are fed up with flooding Aida Havel mulled her fate over coffee after working the early voting polls all day in Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina. “We are trapped,” she concluded. The Dare county commission candidate lives about 50 miles (80km) south, on Hatteras Island on the state’s Outer Banks.
summary: At more than $52m, the race has become the most expensive in US history, but residents are fed up with flooding Aida Havel mulled her fate over coffee after working the early voting polls all day in Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina. “We are trapped,” she concluded.

title: Simulated heart failure appointments uncover shared consultation patterns among doctors across four countries
content:
An international study led by sociologists Anja Weiß and Tao Liu of the University of Duisburg‑Essen found that doctors in Beijing, Ankara, Groningen and Würzburg treat heart‑failure patients in remarkably similar ways. The research shows that not only are the medical procedures alike, but the questions doctors ask, their gestures and the overall flow of consultations also match across the four cities.

The findings, recently published in Global Networks, highlight a shared clinical culture that may inform discussions about the recognition of foreign medical qualifications.
summary: Whether in Beijing, Ankara, Groningen or Würzburg, doctors treat patients with heart failure in remarkably similar ways. Not only are the medical procedures similar, but so are the questions doctors ask, their gestures and the way consultations unfold.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study links child depression, aggression after 2024 Noto quake to later loneliness
content: The research team led by associate professor Yasuo Murayama of Kanazawa University identified longitudinal associations among loneliness, depressive symptoms, and social behaviors—including aggressive behavior—in children affected by the 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake.
summary: The research found that depressive symptoms and aggressive behavior in children affected by the 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake are associated with later loneliness. The study was led by associate professor Yasuo Murayama of Kanazawa University.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Human dengue trial shows immune memory can help—or backfire
content:
A recent human dengue trial has shown that immune memory can either help or backfire. The study highlights how the body’s response to a first dengue infection may not protect against, and can sometimes worsen, a second infection with a different serotype.

Dengue, transmitted by bites of Aedes mosquitoes, is a viral illness that can produce mild fever, flu‑like symptoms, joint pain, or the severe form known as dengue hemorrhagic fever. What makes the disease particularly dangerous is that a second infection with a different strain can trigger more severe disease rather than stronger immunity.
summary: Dengue is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes and can cause mild to severe symptoms, including dengue hemorrhagic fever. A second infection with a different serotype can result in more severe disease instead of stronger immunity.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Researchers fail to replicate many reported effects of psilocybin in parallel mouse studies
content: Parallel mouse studies failed to replicate many reported effects of psilocybin. Experimental trials of psychedelic drugs in humans and animals have produced conflicting results, raising doubts about their therapeutic role for neurologic or behavioral disorders such as depression and PTSD.
summary: Experimental trials of psychedelic drugs in humans and animals have produced conflicting results. This has created doubts about the therapeutic role of hallucinogens in treating neurologic or behavioral disorders such as depression and PTSD.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Expert Explains Difference Between Vertigo and Dizziness
content:
Vertigo is described as a sensation that either you or your surroundings, or both, are spinning or moving when they are not.  

Neil Shepard, Ph. D., an audiologist at Mayo Clinic in Minnesota, notes that many people confuse vertigo with dizziness, but the two are distinct.
summary: Vertigo is a sensation that either you or your surroundings, or both, are spinning or moving when they are not. Some people confuse vertigo with dizziness, but there is a difference, explains Neil Shepard, Ph.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Mechanical thrombectomy linked to lower mortality in intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism
content: New research presented at TCT 2026 and simultaneously published in JSCAI found that, in the primary analysis, mechanical thrombectomy was associated with lower short‑ and long‑term mortality among patients with intermediate‑risk pulmonary embolism compared with anticoagulation alone.
summary: New research presented at TCT 2026 and simultaneously published in JSCAI found that mechanical thrombectomy was associated with lower short- and long-term mortality among patients with intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism. The study compared mechanical thrombectomy to anticoagulation alone.

content: Close your eyes and cover your ears. Much of the world around you disappears from view and hearing, yet your sense of being present, of being conscious, remains. What creates that basic feeling of being "you"?

Digital streamers and traditional television networks are now competing for midterm coverage, with journalists such as Jim Acosta and Scott MacFarlane turning their attention to their former employers for viewership.  

For the first time in more than two decades, Acosta—who left CNN last year after nearly 18 years with the network—will not be on a mainstream television channel on election night.  Instead, he will host his own live broadcast from the University of Virginia, which will stream on YouTube and on his Substack platform.
summary: Jim Acosta, a former CNN stalwart, will not be working for a mainstream television network on election night. He is putting on his own live broadcast at the University of Virginia that will air on YouTube and his Substack platform.

Drivers are filling up less, she said, while ringing people up for cigarettes and beer, and fewer people are buying a full tank. Some stop once they’ve reached $10 or $20 worth of gasoline.

content: A University of Queensland study has shown that laboratory-based propagation of avocado does not carry an inherent environmental cost. Led by researchers from the Queensland Alliance for Agriculture and Food Innovation and industry partners, the study presents the first integrated environmental comparison between plant tissue culture–based clonal rootstock propagation and conventional seedling propagation.

content: Statistician Andrea Riebler identified a Chinese vendor selling software that rapidly mines public health data, a discovery she made after noting a surge in citations of her work. The tool enables users to generate ready-to-publish research papers in under two hours. This development threatens the integrity of the peer-review system, as scientific papers represent a researcher’s most valuable currency and often reflect years of dedicated effort.

After noting a surge in citations of her work, statistician Andrea Riebler discovered a vendor in China selling a tool that enables rapid paper mining of public health data.

content: Urban flooding inflicts substantial social, environmental, and economic damage annually. In Baltimore, these losses have grown in both frequency and intensity since records began in 1748, with further increases anticipated due to climate change. Conventional flood prevention methods, which rely on concrete and other impervious surfaces to manage water flow, frequently prove ineffective in urban areas because they prevent rainwater from infiltrating the ground.
summary: Urban flooding in Baltimore has caused significant social, environmental, and economic losses, with frequency and intensity increasing since records began in 1748. Traditional flood prevention approaches that use concrete and other impervious surfaces fail in urban settings because they impede rainwater infiltration.

title: Pearls and Bird Feathers Inspire Simpler Method for Producing Structural Colors
content:
Colors in nature are not always produced by pigments. Pearls, bird feathers, butterfly wings and opals display brilliant colors.  

These hues arise from light interacting with microscopic structures, a phenomenon known as structural color.
summary: Colors in nature can be produced by structural color rather than pigments. Pearls, bird feathers, butterfly wings and opals display brilliant colors through light interacting with microscopic structures.

content: A decade‑long study of museum specimens uncovered two previously unrecognized bandicoot species. The work also expanded the known range of the iconic quenda (or southeastern brown bandicoot) and reshaped understanding of one of Australia’s native mammal groups.

title: Early humans settled only along Arabian desert margins despite interior lakes
content:
Models of early population migrations assume people moved to places with easy access to water. That assumption has created a puzzling gap in our understanding of ancient Arabia.

Evidence shows monsoon rains once filled lakes and supported grasslands in the vast sandy interior, yet archaeological evidence of early human occupation is concentrated almost entirely around the desert margins.
summary: Models of early population migrations assume people moved to places with easy access to water. Yet evidence shows early human occupation in ancient Arabia is concentrated almost entirely around desert margins, even though monsoon rains once filled lakes and supported grasslands in the interior.

content: Your body uses collagen to give skin strength and elasticity, so taking collagen supplements appears to be a logical way to reduce wrinkles. Columnist Alice Klein, however, argues that the situation is not that straightforward.

title: MIT researchers use super‑flexible ligands to create customizable nanoparticle materials
content:
Researchers from MIT and the University of Delaware have developed a new method for assembling nanoparticles into designer materials, published in Nature Materials. The approach utilizes super-flexible connector molecules, or ligands, that intentionally deform based on their surrounding environment to regulate the packing of nanoparticle networks. By leveraging connector flexibility and electric charges, the team demonstrated how to tune the structure of these networks, creating new kinds of nanoparticle-based materials. This technique aims to overcome previous limitations in controlling the number and direction of links between particles, offering a more versatile pathway for applications in photonics, chemical catalysis, medicine, and agriculture.

Traditional methods for creating nanoparticle superlattices often relied on changing particle shapes or aligning rigid connector chains. However, these approaches limited the possible material structures and were difficult to scale because they required specific, bespoke synthesis methods that worked only under certain conditions. Rob Macfarlane, the Richard P. Simmons (1953) Professor in Metallurgy in MIT’s Department of Materials Science and Engineering, noted that the prevailing dogma for 20 years was that connector ligands needed to be rigid to prevent assembly failure. The new research challenges this view by demonstrating that extreme flexibility can be just as effective, allowing ligands to reorganize as particles come together.

In the new system, the nanoparticles feature flexible ligands with electrically charged tips, where positive and negative charges attract one another. This allows the bonds to be as flexible as desired, spontaneously moving toward configurations that maximize bond stability. Experiments led by MIT PhD candidate Nicholas Sbalbi showed that researchers could control the connections by altering nanoparticle sizes and ligand chain lengths. The amount of polymer flexibility dictates the number of bonds each particle forms, enabling the creation of lattices with fewer bonds per particle than previously possible using rigid connectors.

The team successfully assembled the nanoparticles into previously unseen crystal structures without needing to predesign specific connection points or particle shapes. Macfarlane explained that this method allows for less dense formations of nanoparticles, which opens up interesting applications that are limited by traditional dense packing. The researchers believe this establishes ligand flexibility as a new path for customizing material structures at scale, moving toward independent control over both the particle properties and the resulting assembly.

In addition to Macfarlane and Sbalbi, the paper includes contributions from University of Delaware doctoral student Stephen Kronenberger, MIT undergraduate Hana Shinzawa, Matthew Ye PhD ’26, and former University of Delaware professor Arthi Jayaraman. The research was supported in part by the National Science Foundation, the Department of Energy, the U.S. Army, and the U.S. Navy.
summary: Creating better-performing materials comes down to having more control over their structure at the smallest possible scale. One particularly effective way to accomplish that is using nanoparticles, which have highly customizable shapes and sizes and have already shown promise in applications across energy, medicine, and electronics.
